explanation: PM² suggests six **Project Management Plans**: the **Requirements Management Plan**, the **Project Change Management Plan**, the **Risk Management Plan**, the **Quality Management Plan**, the **Issue Management Plan** and the **Communications Management Plan**. The **Outsourcing Plan** is not among them — it is a project-specific plan with its own section and its own RASCI row. B is the tempting distractor, but the **Communications Management Plan** is explicitly the sixth plan on the list.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English; answer key and page reference verified against the guide, no change needed.

question: Where should the escalation procedure and tolerances be defined and tailored?

options.A: In the Business Case
options.B: In each Management Plan separately, with no cross-reference
options.C: In the Project Charter
options.D: In the Project Handbook, referenced by the Management Plans to ensure a consistent approach

explanation: An escalation procedure and tolerances should be defined (and tailored) in the **Project Handbook**, and this should be referenced by the **Management Plans** so that a consistent approach is applied across the project. B is the tempting distractor: the **Management Plans** do cover escalation, but by reference to the **Project Handbook** rather than by defining it separately, which would duplicate information and risk inconsistency.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English; answer key and page reference verified against the guide, no change needed.

question: Which groups of standard project roles are included in the PM² Project Stakeholder Matrix template?

options.A: Initiating, Planning, Executing and Closing
options.B: Teams, Roles, Support, Operational roles and Other domain-specific
options.C: Responsible, Accountable, Supports, Consulted and Informed
options.D: Directing, Managing, Performing and Business Governing

explanation: The PM² **Project Stakeholder Matrix** template organises the standard project roles into five groups: **Teams** (e.g. the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)**), **Roles** (e.g. **Project Owner (PO)**, **Solution Provider (SP)**, **User Representatives (URs)**), **Support** (e.g. **Project Support Office (PSO)**, **Project Manager Assistant (PMA)**), **Operational roles** (e.g. user, business analyst) and **Other domain-specific** (e.g. architect). D is the tempting distractor because Business Governing, Directing, Managing and Performing are genuine PM² governance layers, but they are not the grouping used in this template; C lists the RASCI responsibility levels instead.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English; answer key and page reference verified against the guide, no change needed.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Project Stakeholder Matrix, what is the role of the Business Implementation Group (BIG)?

options.A: Responsible
options.B: Consulted
options.C: Supports
options.D: Informed

explanation: The **Project Stakeholder Matrix** RASCI row reads AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=S, BIG=**C**, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=C — identical to the **Project Handbook** row — so the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** is **Consulted**. C is the tempting distractor: **Supports** is the **Business Manager (BM)**, who assists the **Project Manager (PM)**, particularly with identifying stakeholders on the client side.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English; answer key and page verified (Appendix E confirms BIG=C), no change needed.

question: The Project Work Plan is composed of which three parts?

options.A: Deliverables Breakdown, Risk Log and Gantt Chart
options.B: Work Breakdown, Effort & Cost Estimates, and Project Schedule
options.C: Scope, Time and Cost
options.D: Work Breakdown, Quality Plan and Communications Plan

explanation: The **Project Work Plan** is composed of three parts: the **Work Breakdown**, the **Effort & Cost Estimates** and the **Project Schedule**. It should be baselined and also kept up to date throughout the life of the project. A is the tempting distractor, but the **Risk Log** is a separate **Project Log** and a Gantt chart is only one way of presenting the **Project Schedule**; C names the project objectives, not the parts of the plan.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English; answer key and page reference verified against the guide, no change needed.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Project Work Plan, what is the role of the Project Core Team (PCT)?

options.A: R
options.B: I
options.C: S/C
options.D: C

explanation: The **Project Work Plan** RASCI row reads AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S/C, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=**S/C**. The **Project Core Team (PCT)** assists the **Project Manager (PM)** in developing the plan, so it is both **Supports** and **Consulted**. D is the tempting distractor: plain **C** is the value for the **Project Owner (PO)**, the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** and the **Solution Provider (SP)**, while the **PCT** carries the combined **S/C** it shares with the **Business Manager (BM)**.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English; answer key and page verified (Appendix E confirms PCT=S/C), no change needed.

question: Which statement about the Outsourcing Plan is correct?

options.A: It is prepared by the Solution Provider (SP) and reviewed by the Project Manager (PM)
options.B: It is prepared by the Contractor's Project Manager (CPM)
options.C: It replaces the organisational procurement rules and procedures
options.D: It is prepared by the Project Manager (PM) and reviewed by the Solution Provider (SP)

explanation: The **Project Manager (PM)** prepares the **Outsourcing Plan** and the **Solution Provider (SP)** reviews it, so D is right. The plan must be compliant with the relevant organisational procurement rules and procedures, which are also one of its inputs. C is wrong because compliance is the opposite of replacement: the **Outsourcing Plan** never overrides the organisation's procurement rules. A simply reverses the two roles.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Outsourcing Plan, which role is Accountable?

options.A: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: The Solution Provider (SP)
options.C: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)
options.D: The Project Owner (PO)

explanation: The **Outsourcing Plan** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=A, PSC=C, PO=C, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=S, PM=R, PCT=I**, so the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** is Accountable. This is one of only two rows in the whole methodology where the **AGB** is Accountable, the other being **Manage Outsourcing** in **Monitor & Control**. A is the tempting answer because the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** is Accountable for most other Planning artefacts, but here it is only Consulted.

question: Which statement about the Deliverables Acceptance Plan is correct?

options.A: Acceptance activities are excluded from the Project Work Plan to avoid duplication
options.B: Deliverables acceptance activities always happen only at the end of the Executing Phase
options.C: The plan is prepared by the Business Manager (BM) and approved by the Solution Provider (SP)
options.D: Deliverables acceptance activities may not happen only at the end of the Executing Phase, but can follow the project's delivery schedule

explanation: The guidelines state that deliverables acceptance activities may not happen (only) at the end of the **Executing Phase** but can follow the project's delivery schedule, which makes D correct and B wrong. The same guidelines require those activities and the resources they need to be included in the **Project Work Plan**, so A states the opposite of the rule. C is wrong on both counts: the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan** is prepared by the **Project Manager (PM)** and approved by the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)**, while the **Business Manager (BM)** only reviews and validates the acceptance requirements, activities and metrics.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Deliverables Acceptance Plan, what is the role of the Business Implementation Group (BIG)?

options.A: Supports
options.B: Informed
options.C: Consulted
options.D: Accountable

explanation: The **Deliverables Acceptance Plan** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=I, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C**, so the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** is Informed. C (Consulted) is the trap: the **BIG** is Consulted on the **Transition Plan** and the **Business Implementation Plan**, but only Informed on this one. A (Supports) is the **Business Manager (BM)**'s role in this same row, not the **BIG**'s.

question: What is the purpose of the Transition Plan?

options.A: To document the impact of the project on the organisation's processes, culture and people and the change-management activities required
options.B: To define the goals, prerequisites, activities and responsibilities associated with transitioning from the old (pre-project) to the new (post-project) state
options.C: To describe the contracting strategies used to procure services outside the organisation
options.D: To define the criteria and approach for the formal acceptance of deliverables

explanation: The **Transition Plan** defines the goals, prerequisites, activities and responsibilities associated with transitioning from the old (pre-project) to the new (post-project) state, minimising business disruption during the transition. A is the **Business Implementation Plan**, not the **Transition Plan**: it documents the project's impact on the organisation's processes, culture and people and the change-management activities required. C describes the **Outsourcing Plan** and D the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan**.

question: Step 8 of the Transition Plan requires defining and scheduling the transfer of responsibility for the deliverables from which role to which role?

options.A: From the Project Core Team (PCT) to the Business Implementation Group (BIG)
options.B: From the Contractor's Project Manager (CPM) to the Project Manager (PM)
options.C: From the Project Manager (PM) to the Business Manager (BM)
options.D: From the Solution Provider (SP) to the Project Owner (PO)

explanation: Step 8 of the **Transition Plan** is to define and schedule the transfer of responsibility for the deliverables from the **Solution Provider (SP)** to the **Project Owner (PO)**. C is the tempting distractor, but the handover is not from the **Project Manager (PM)** to the **Business Manager (BM)**: the **PO** is the role that takes the finished deliverables into its care, custody and control, as **Administrative Closure** confirms. A and B name transfers the guide never describes.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Transition Plan, what is the role of the Business Manager (BM)?

options.A: Accountable
options.B: Supports
options.C: Consulted
options.D: Responsible

explanation: The **Transition Plan** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=C, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C**, so the **Business Manager (BM)** is Consulted. In this row every role other than the **AGB** (Informed), the **PSC** (Accountable) and the **PM** (Responsible) is Consulted. B (Supports) is the trap: **S** is the **BM**'s role in the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan** and the **Project-End Review Meeting**, but not in the **Transition Plan**.

question: Who prepares the Business Implementation Plan and who approves it?

options.A: Prepared by the Business Implementation Group (BIG), approved by the Business Manager (BM)
options.B: Prepared by the Solution Provider (SP), approved by the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)
options.C: Prepared by the Business Manager (BM), approved by the Project Owner (PO)
options.D: Prepared by the Project Manager (PM), approved by the Project Steering Committee (PSC)

explanation: The **Business Manager (BM)** prepares the **Business Implementation Plan**, assisted by the **Project Manager (PM)**, who updates the **Project Work Plan** to include the business implementation activities; the **Project Owner (PO)** reviews and approves it. The RAM (RASCI) row confirms this: **PO=A, BM=R, PM=S**. D is the trap because **PM** prepares / **PSC** approves is the pattern for most Planning artefacts, but this artefact is one of the exceptions. The **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** in A is only Consulted during the impact analysis.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Business Implementation Plan, what is the role of the Project Manager (PM)?

options.A: Supports
options.B: Accountable
options.C: Responsible
options.D: Consulted

explanation: The **Business Implementation Plan** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=R, BIG=C, SP=I, PM=S, PCT=I**, so the **Project Manager (PM)** Supports. C (Responsible) is the reflex answer because the **PM** is **R** on nearly every other artefact, but here **R** belongs to the **Business Manager (BM)**, who prepares the plan. The same split appears in **Manage Business Implementation** in **Monitor & Control**.

question: At the RfE (Ready for Executing) gate, what must happen if major deviations from the approved Business Case and/or Project Charter are identified?

options.A: The project must return to the Initiating Phase
options.B: The Project Manager (PM) may approve the deviations directly
options.C: The Project Owner (PO) must re-baseline the Project Work Plan without further approval
options.D: The Project Steering Committee (PSC) must receive an additional approval from the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) before the project can move on to the Executing Phase

explanation: At the **RfE (Ready for Executing)** gate the **Project Manager (PM)** assesses whether the Planning Phase goals have been achieved and requests approval from the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** to move to the **Executing Phase**. If major deviations from the approved **Business Case** and/or **Project Charter** are identified, the **PSC** must receive an additional approval from the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** first. A is the trap: PM² escalates upward to the **AGB**, it does not send the project back to the **Initiating Phase**.

question: How does the Executing Phase begin and end?

options.A: It begins with the approval of the Project Charter and ends with administrative closure
options.B: It begins with a Kick-off Meeting and ends with the acceptance (final or provisional, as per the Deliverables Acceptance Plan) by the requestor side
options.C: It begins with the Project-End Review Meeting and ends with the Project-End Report
options.D: It begins with the Planning Kick-off Meeting and ends with the RfE gate

explanation: The **Executing Phase** begins with a **Kick-off Meeting** and ends with the acceptance (final or provisional, as per the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan**) by the requestor side; during the phase the deliverables are produced and the requestor organisation prepares for their introduction. D is the trap: beginning with the **Planning Kick-off Meeting** and ending at the **RfE** gate describes the **Planning Phase**. Administrative closure in A belongs to the **Closing Phase**, and the **Project-End Review Meeting** in C opens the **Closing Phase**.

question: Which of the following must be presented during the Executing Kick-off Meeting?

options.A: The Project Handbook, the Project Work Plan, the Communications Management Plan and the Project Stakeholder Matrix
options.B: The Business Case and the cost-benefit analysis of alternatives
options.C: The Project-End Report and the Lessons Learned
options.D: The Deliverables Acceptance Note and the Project Acceptance Note

explanation: During the **Executing Kick-off Meeting** the **Project Manager (PM)** presents the **Project Handbook** and the **Project Work Plan**, the **Communications Management Plan** and the **Project Stakeholder Matrix**, plus the **Risk Management**, **Issue Management** and **Project Change Management** processes and the **Quality Assurance & Control** activities, and the team agrees its ground rules. B is the trap: the **Business Case** and the cost-benefit analysis of alternatives belong to the **Initiating Phase** and are only an input here, not something presented. C and D name **Closing** and acceptance artefacts that do not exist yet at kick-off.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Executing Kick-off Meeting, what is the role of the Business Manager (BM)?

options.A: Consulted (C)
options.B: Supports (S)
options.C: Supports/Consulted (S/C)
options.D: Responsible (R)

explanation: The **Executing Kick-off Meeting** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S/C, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C**, so the **Business Manager (BM)** is **S/C** (Supports/Consulted). B (plain Supports) is the trap: **S** is the **BM**'s role at the **Planning Kick-off Meeting**, which becomes **S/C** at the **Executing Kick-off Meeting**. **R** belongs to the **PM** and the **PSC** is the Accountable role in this row.
changes: Options rewritten to spell out the RASCI letters (option letters collided with RASCI codes, e.g. answer 'C' vs option content 'C'); distractor B changed from 'I' to 'Supports (S)' so it tests the Planning vs Executing kick-off nuance. Key unchanged (C).

question: When does project coordination officially begin and end?

options.A: It runs only during the Executing Phase
options.B: It begins with the Planning Phase and ends when the Project Work Plan is baselined
options.C: It begins officially with the initiation of the project and ends with its closing, though its intensity peaks during the Executing Phase
options.D: It begins with the Executing Kick-off Meeting and ends at the RfC gate

explanation: The note under **Project Coordination** states that project coordination begins officially with the initiation of the project and ends with its closing, although its intensity peaks during the **Executing Phase**. A is the trap: coordination is documented in the **Executing** chapter and peaks there, but it is not confined to that phase. The **PM** coordinates all project activities, assisted by the **Project Manager Assistant (PMA)** and supported by the **Business Manager (BM)**.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Project Coordination, which role is Accountable and which is Responsible?

options.A: PSC Accountable, PM Responsible
options.B: SP Accountable, PM Responsible
options.C: PO Accountable, PM Responsible
options.D: PM Accountable, PCT Responsible

explanation: The **Project Coordination** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=S, BIG=I, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=I**, so the **Project Owner (PO)** is Accountable and the **Project Manager (PM)** Responsible. A is the trap: the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** is Accountable for the **Executing Kick-off Meeting**, but for the ongoing Executing activities accountability sits with the **PO**. D is the **Quality Assurance** row (**PM=A, PCT=R**), not this one.

question: How does PM² define Quality Assurance?

options.A: The process of managing versions of artefacts and preventing unauthorised changes
options.B: The activity of gathering evidence that proves the project work is following high-quality standards, methodologies and best practices
options.C: The activity of monitoring and consolidating the results of Quality Assurance in order to assess compliance and performance
options.D: The formal acceptance of deliverables by the Project Owner (PO)

explanation: PM² defines **Quality Assurance** as the activity of gathering evidence that proves the project work is following high-quality standards, methodologies and best practices, giving confidence that the project will satisfy the desired scope and quality requirements within the project constraints. A is **configuration management**, a procedure documented in the **Quality Management Plan** that ensures correct versions are delivered and prevents unauthorised changes, not **Quality Assurance**. C is the guide's definition of **Quality Control**, which monitors and consolidates the results of **Quality Assurance** to assess compliance and performance, i.e. the downstream half of the pair.
changes: Option C rewritten to the guide's exact definition of Quality Control (was a vaguer, non-PM2 phrasing), making the QA/QC contrast the real trap. Key unchanged (B).

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Quality Assurance in the Executing Phase, which role is Responsible?

options.A: The Project Core Team (PCT)
options.B: The Project Quality Assurance (PQA)
options.C: The Project Manager (PM)
options.D: The Solution Provider (SP)

explanation: The **Quality Assurance** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=I, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=I, PM=A, PCT=R**, so the **Project Core Team (PCT)** is Responsible: it must provide evidence of adherence to the quality assurance standards. C is the trap: the **Project Manager (PM)** is Accountable for carrying out all **Quality Assurance** activities, and this is the only row in the **Executing Phase** where the **PM** is Accountable rather than Responsible. The **Project Quality Assurance (PQA)** in B establishes the standards and reviews outputs, but it is not one of the eight RAM columns.

question: Which report is filled out by the contractor and submitted to the Project Manager (PM) according to the agreed schedule?

options.A: The Quality Review Report
options.B: The Project Progress Report
options.C: The Contractor Status Report
options.D: The Project Status Report

explanation: The **Contractor Status Report** is filled out by the contractor (if there is one) and submitted to the **Project Manager (PM)** in accordance with the agreed schedule, covering the current reporting period, forecasts and any new risks, disputes and issues. The **PM** must then include a summary of the **Contractor Status Reports** in the **Project Status Report**. D is the trap: the **Project Status Report** is produced by the **PM** and submitted to the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)**, not filled out by the contractor.
changes: Page corrected 59 -> 60 (the Contractor Status Report description is on p60; p59 holds only the report list and the RASCI row).

question: For a multi-annual project whose overall vision/scope has NOT changed, which artefact can be used to secure project approval for the following year?

options.A: The Project Status Report
options.B: An updated Project Charter
options.C: The Business Case
options.D: The Project Progress Report

explanation: If a project is multi-annual and its overall vision/scope has not changed, the **Project Progress Report** can be used to secure project approval for the following year. B is the trap: an updated **Project Charter** is required only when the project's vision/scope has changed. The **Project Status Report** in A summarises performance for a reporting period and is not an approval instrument.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Project Reporting, what are the roles of the Business Implementation Group (BIG) and the Solution Provider (SP)?

options.A: BIG is I and SP is C
options.B: Both are S/C
options.C: Both are C
options.D: Both are I/C

explanation: The **Project Reporting** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=S/C, BIG=I/C, SP=I/C, PM=R, PCT=C**, so both the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** and the **Solution Provider (SP)** are **I/C**. This is the only row in the methodology that uses the **I/C** notation. B is the trap: **S/C** is the **Business Manager (BM)**'s role in this same row, not the **BIG**'s or the **SP**'s.

question: Which role 'manages internal communication and assists in activities such as document change control and baselining of plans' in the Information Distribution activity?

options.A: The Project Quality Assurance (PQA)
options.B: The Project Core Team (PCT)
options.C: The Business Manager (BM)
options.D: The Project Support Office (PSO)

explanation: In the **Information Distribution** activity the **Project Support Office (PSO)** manages internal communication and assists in activities such as document change control and the baselining of plans. B is the trap: in that same table the **Project Manager (PM)** ensures the **Project Core Team (PCT)** has all the information it needs to carry out its tasks, so the **PCT** receives information rather than managing document control. The **Project Quality Assurance (PQA)** in A is not named in this activity at all.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Information Distribution, what is the role of the Business Manager (BM)?

options.A: Supports
options.B: Consulted
options.C: Responsible
options.D: Informed

explanation: The **Information Distribution** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=C**, so the **Business Manager (BM)** is Consulted. A (Supports) is the trap: the **BM** is **S** in **Project Coordination** and **S/C** in **Project Reporting**, but only **C** in **Information Distribution**. **R** belongs to the **PM** and **A** to the **Project Owner (PO)**.

question: At the RfC (Ready for Closing) gate, what is the Project Manager (PM) also responsible for ensuring?

options.A: That all Lessons Learned have been archived
options.B: That the Project Owner (PO) accepts the deliverables (at least provisionally), that the transition is finalised and that the outputs are made available to the end-users
options.C: That the Business Case is re-approved by the Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.D: That the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) re-baselines the budget

explanation: At the **RfC (Ready for Closing)** gate the **Project Manager (PM)** verifies that all **Executing Phase** goals have been achieved, all planned activities carried out, all requirements met and all outputs fully delivered, and is also responsible for ensuring that the **Project Owner (PO)** accepts the deliverables (at least provisionally), that the transition is finalised and that the outputs are made available to the end-users. The **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** can then authorise the move to the **Closing Phase**. A is the trap: archiving documentation, including the **Lessons Learned**, is **Administrative Closure** work performed after this gate, in the **Closing Phase**.

question: How does the Closing Phase start and end?

options.A: It starts with the Project Acceptance Note and ends with the release of resources
options.B: It starts with administrative closure and ends with the Lessons Learned session
options.C: It starts with the RfC gate and ends with the Project-End Report
options.D: It starts with the Project-End Review Meeting and ends with the Project Owner's (PO) final approval, which marks the project's administrative closure

explanation: The **Closing Phase** starts with the **Project-End Review Meeting** and ends with the **Project Owner's (PO)** final approval, which marks the project's administrative closure. C is the trap: the **RfC (Ready for Closing)** gate closes the **Executing Phase** and precedes the **Closing Phase**, and the **Project-End Report** is produced during the phase rather than ending it. The release of resources and archiving in A and B are **Administrative Closure** steps inside the phase, not its boundaries.

question: Which of the following is a goal of the Project-End Review Meeting?

options.A: To approve the final invoice of the contractor
options.B: To formally accept each interim deliverable
options.C: To baseline the Project Work Plan for the operations period
options.D: To ensure project members discuss their experience so that Lessons Learned and best practices can be captured, to evaluate team and contractor performance, and to discuss ideas and recommendations for post-project work

explanation: The goal of the **Project-End Review Meeting** is to ensure project members discuss their experience of the project so that **Lessons Learned** and best practices can be captured; team and contractor performance are evaluated and ideas and recommendations for post-project work are discussed. B is the trap: formal acceptance of deliverables is governed by the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan** and happens during the **Executing Phase**, not at this meeting. A and C describe contractual and planning actions the guide never assigns to this meeting.

question: Why does PM² suggest that the Lessons Learned session be facilitated by someone who has not been intimately involved in the project?

options.A: To reduce the cost of the session
options.B: Because the Project Manager (PM) is not allowed to attend
options.C: To comply with audit requirements
options.D: To allow the Project Manager (PM) to contribute as a participant

explanation: The guidelines state that it may be preferable to have the **Lessons Learned** session facilitated by someone who has not been intimately involved in the project, allowing the **Project Manager (PM)** to contribute as a participant. B is the trap and says the opposite: the **PM** does attend; the external facilitator exists precisely so the **PM** can take part instead of running the session. The **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** should also be invited so its members can transfer the lessons to other projects.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Lessons Learned and Post-Project Recommendations, which role is Accountable?

options.A: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: The Project Manager (PM)
options.C: The Project Core Team (PCT)
options.D: The Project Owner (PO)

explanation: The **Lessons Learned and Post-Project Recommendations** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C**, identical to the **Project-End Review Meeting** and **Project-End Report** rows, so the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** is Accountable. D is the trap: the **Project Owner (PO)** is Accountable only for **Administrative Closure** among the four **Closing Phase** activities and is merely Consulted here. The **PM** is Responsible for organising the gathering of lessons.

question: Who writes the Project-End Report, and who provides input and assistance?

options.A: Written by the Project Manager (PM), with input from the Project Quality Assurance (PQA) and the Project Core Team (PCT)
options.B: Written by the Business Manager (BM), with input from the Business Implementation Group (BIG)
options.C: Written by the Project Steering Committee (PSC), with input from the Solution Provider (SP)
options.D: Written by the Project Support Office (PSO), with input from the Project Owner (PO)

explanation: The **Project-End Report** is written by the **Project Manager (PM)**, with the **Project Quality Assurance (PQA)** and the **Project Core Team (PCT)** providing input and assistance; its main input is the **Minutes of Meeting (MoM)** of the **Project-End Review Meeting**. D is the trap: the **Project Support Office (PSO)** assists in reviewing, organising and archiving documentation during **Administrative Closure**, but it does not write this report. The **Business Manager (BM)** in B represents the business side at the review meeting rather than authoring the report.

question: What does formal project closure allow, according to the Administrative Closure section?

options.A: It authorises the Project Manager (PM) to re-baseline the schedule
options.B: It transfers accountability for benefits to the Project Core Team (PCT)
options.C: It triggers the Business Implementation Plan
options.D: It brings project mode to an end and allows operations mode to commence

explanation: The project is officially closed once all **Closing Phase** activities are completed and the **Project Owner (PO)** has approved the project; formal project closure brings project mode to an end and allows operations mode to commence. C is the trap: the **Business Implementation Plan** is produced in the **Planning Phase** and its activities are scheduled and controlled as part of the **Project Work Plan**, so closure does not trigger it. B is wrong because closure transfers the deliverables into the care, custody and control of the **PO**, not accountability for benefits to the **Project Core Team (PCT)**.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Administrative Closure, what are the roles of the Project Steering Committee (PSC) and the Project Owner (PO)?

options.A: PSC = A, PO = R
options.B: PSC = A, PO = C
options.C: PSC = I, PO = A
options.D: PSC = C, PO = A

explanation: The **Administrative Closure** RAM (RASCI) row reads **AGB=I, PSC=C, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=I**, so the **Project Owner (PO)** is Accountable and the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** only Consulted. The **PO** is Accountable because it has final approval of the project and closes it. B is the trap: the **PSC** is Accountable for the other three **Closing Phase** activities (**Project-End Review Meeting**, **Lessons Learned and Post-Project Recommendations**, **Project-End Report**), but not for **Administrative Closure**.

question: Which checklists does PM² provide to help the Project Manager (PM) control the project?

options.A: Risk, Issue, Change and Decision Checklists
options.B: Initiating, Planning, Executing and Closing Checklists
options.C: Requirements, Communications, Outsourcing and Quality Checklists
options.D: Phase-exit Review, Quality Review, Deliverables Acceptance, Transition, Stakeholders and Business Implementation Checklists

explanation: PM² provides six **Checklists** to help the **Project Manager (PM)** control the project: **Phase-exit Review Checklist**, **Quality Review Checklist**, **Deliverables Acceptance Checklist**, **Transition Checklist**, **Stakeholders Checklist** and **Business Implementation Checklist**. D reproduces that list exactly. A is the tempting distractor: Risk, Issue, Change and Decision are the four **Project Logs**, not checklists. B names the four phases and C names Project Management Plans.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Monitor Project Performance, what is the role of the Solution Provider (SP)?

options.A: Accountable
options.B: Consulted
options.C: Supports
options.D: Informed

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for **Monitor Project Performance** reads AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=C, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=C, so the **Solution Provider (SP)** is **Informed**. **Control Schedule** and **Control Cost** carry the identical row. B is the trap: **Consulted** on this row belongs to the **Business Manager (BM)**, the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** and the **Project Core Team (PCT)**, while **Accountable** (A) is the **Project Owner (PO)**.

question: According to Control Schedule, what must happen if the schedule is at risk or considerable delays are foreseen beyond the predefined thresholds?

options.A: The Project Steering Committee (PSC) needs to be informed and corrective actions must be devised, agreed and implemented; affected stakeholders should also be notified
options.B: The project moves directly to the Closing Phase
options.C: The Project Manager (PM) re-baselines the schedule without informing anyone
options.D: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) takes over the project

explanation: **Control Schedule** states that if the schedule is at risk or considerable delays are foreseen beyond the predefined thresholds, the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** must be informed, corrective actions must be devised, agreed and implemented, and affected project stakeholders must also be notified. A states that rule. C is the tempting distractor: the **Project Manager (PM)** updates the schedule for approved changes, but significant deviations are escalated, never re-baselined silently. D is wrong because the **AGB** approves a considerable **budget** revision under **Control Cost**, not schedule slippage.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: If the project budget needs to be considerably revised, whose formal approval is required before the affected plans can be re-baselined?

options.A: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: The Project Owner (PO)
options.C: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)
options.D: The Solution Provider (SP)

explanation: Step 5 of **Control Cost** requires formal approval from the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** before the affected plans can be re-baselined when the project budget has to be considerably revised. B is the most tempting distractor: the **Project Owner (PO)** owns and approves the budgeted costs and approves significant differences between budgeted and actual costs (steps 2-3), but not the re-baselining. The **PSC** (A) is only informed when the budget is at risk.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: When does the Manage Stakeholders activity begin and end?

options.A: It begins in the Initiating Phase, when project expectations and requirements are identified, and ends in the Closing Phase, when stakeholders' overall project experience and satisfaction are recorded
options.B: It begins in the Executing Phase and ends when the deliverables are accepted
options.C: It runs only during Monitor & Control activities in the Executing Phase
options.D: It begins in the Planning Phase and ends at the RfE gate

explanation: **Manage Stakeholders** begins in the **Initiating Phase**, when project expectations and requirements are identified, and ends in the **Closing Phase**, when stakeholders' overall project experience and satisfaction are recorded. Responsibility belongs to the **Project Manager (PM)**, helped by the **Business Manager (BM)** on the requestor (user) side. C is the trap: stakeholder management is one of the **Monitor & Control** activities, which peak during the **Executing Phase**, but the guide explicitly spans the activity from Initiating to Closing.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Manage Stakeholders, what are the roles of the Business Implementation Group (BIG) and the Solution Provider (SP)?

D is the trap because it inverts them: on most other **Monitor & Control** rows (**Manage Requirements**, **Manage Risks**, **Manage Issues and Decisions**) the **BIG** is **Consulted** and the **SP** is **Informed**. **Manage Stakeholders** reverses that pattern.

question: Who assesses whether the implemented solution satisfies the initial business need in step 5 of the requirements management process?

options.A: The User Representatives (URs)
options.B: The Business Manager (BM)
options.C: The Project Quality Assurance (PQA)
options.D: The Project Core Team (PCT)

B is the tempting distractor: the **Business Manager (BM)** provides the information needed to draft the requirements and approves them (step 3), but does not perform the validation of the implemented solution.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Manage Requirements, what is the role of the Project Core Team (PCT)?

question: In the Manage Project Change process, what are the four possible decisions when approving a change?

options.A: Accept, avoid, transfer or reduce the change request
options.B: Approve, reject, postpone or merge the change request
options.C: Submit, assess, approve or implement the change request
options.D: Approve, escalate, implement or close the change request

explanation: Step 3 of **Manage Project Change**, *Approve the change*, gives exactly four possible decisions: **approve**, **reject**, **postpone** or **merge** the change request. The decision details are documented in the **Change Log** and communicated to the requestor. A is the classic trap: avoid, transfer/share, reduce and accept are the **risk-response strategies** for threats, not change decisions. C lists process steps rather than decisions.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Manage Project Change, what is the role of the Project Steering Committee (PSC)?

options.A: Accountable
options.B: Consulted
options.C: Informed
options.D: Supports

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for **Manage Project Change** reads AGB=I, PSC=C, PO=A, BM=S, BIG=I, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=C, so the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** is **Consulted**. question: Which risk-response strategies apply to positive risks (opportunities) in PM²?

options.A: Identify, Assess, Respond, Control
options.B: Mitigate, Escalate, Reject, Merge
options.C: Avoid, Reduce, Accept, Transfer/Share
options.D: Exploit, Enhance, Accept, Share

explanation: The **Risk Log** lists the strategies for negative risks (threats) as **Avoid, Reduce, Accept, Transfer/Share** and the strategies for positive risks (opportunities) as **Exploit, Enhance, Accept, Share**. D is the opportunities list. C is the most tempting distractor because it is the threats list and because **Accept** and **Share** appear in both sets. Step 9 of the **Risk Management Plan** (p. 91) and the *Risk-Response Strategy* glossary entry (p. 137) give the same pairing; the **Manage Risk** section itself does not enumerate them.

question: Which body should be regularly informed about risk-related activities and monitors projects with high levels of risk exposure?

D is the tempting distractor: the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** sits above the project and is only **Informed** on the **Manage Risks** RAM row (AGB=I, PSC=C). The **Project Support Office (PSO)** (B) provides support services and has no risk-monitoring duty in this section.

question: Which log is used to document all relevant decisions taken during the project?

options.A: The Risk Log
options.B: The Change Log
options.C: The Issue Log

question: What is the essential difference between a risk and an issue in PM²?

options.A: A risk is managed by the Project Owner (PO); an issue is managed by the Solution Provider (SP)
options.B: A risk is documented in the Change Log; an issue in the Risk Log
options.C: A risk is an uncertain event that may occur; an issue is an unplanned event that has already happened and requires a project management action
options.D: A risk always has a negative impact; an issue is always positive

explanation: The glossary defines an **issue** as any unplanned event related to the project that has already happened and requires the intervention of the **Project Manager (PM)** or higher management (p. 128), and a **risk** as an uncertain event or set of events, positive or negative, that would affect project objectives should it occur (p. 137). C states that uncertain-versus-already-happened distinction. D is the trap: a risk is explicitly positive **or** negative, since opportunities are risks too, so impact polarity is not what separates the two. B simply swaps the logs: risks go in the **Risk Log**, issues in the **Issue Log**.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Manage Issues and Decisions, what is the role of the Business Manager (BM)?

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Manage Quality, which role is Accountable?

question: Who formally accepts the project's deliverables at the end of the Manage Deliverables Acceptance process?

question: According to PM², can project deliverables be accepted even with known defects or issues?

options.A: Only if the Project Steering Committee (PSC) re-baselines the Deliverables Acceptance Plan first
options.B: Yes, but only after the Closing Phase has started
options.C: No, acceptance requires zero defects
options.D: Yes, they can be conditionally accepted if the defects are documented and there is a plan in place for addressing them

Final project acceptance does take place in the **Closing Phase**, but conditional acceptance of deliverables does not wait for it (B).

question: In the Manage Transition activity, what must the Project Owner (PO) have done before the transition is complete?

question: Who manages the business implementation activities, and who assists?

question: According to Manage Outsourcing, who ensures that the contractor is chosen according to the organisation's processes and standards and that all contracts clearly define the expectations of both parties?

options.A: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)
options.B: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.C: The Solution Provider (SP)
options.D: The Project Manager (PM)

explanation: Steps 1 and 2 of **Manage Outsourcing** assign to the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** the duty to ensure the contractor is chosen according to the organisation's processes and standards and the criteria defined for the project, and that all contracts clearly define the expectations of both parties. D is the most tempting distractor: the **Project Manager (PM)** applies the working methods set out in the **Outsourcing Plan**, monitors costs and schedules and manages changes to the outsourced work (steps 3-6), but does not own contractor selection or contract wording. The **AGB** (A) is **Accountable** on the RAM row, yet the guide names the **PSC** for these two steps.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for Manage Outsourcing, what is the role of the Solution Provider (SP)?

options.A: Responsible
options.B: Supports
options.C: Consulted
options.D: Accountable

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for **Manage Outsourcing** reads AGB=A, PSC=C, PO=C, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=S, PM=R, PCT=I, so the **Solution Provider (SP)** is **Supports** — identical to the **Outsourcing Plan** row. A is the trap: **Responsible** is the **Project Manager (PM)**, who manages the contractor(s). These two outsourcing rows are also the only ones in the PM² RAM where the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** is **Accountable** rather than **Informed**.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: In the absence of a more specialised role, who is responsible for executing the requirements management process from project initiation until all requirements have been implemented and validated?

options.A: The User Representatives (URs)
options.B: The Project Manager (PM)
options.C: The Business Manager (BM)
options.D: The Business Analyst (BA)

explanation: The **Requirements Management Plan** states that, in the absence of a more specialised role, the **Project Manager (PM)** is responsible for executing the requirements management process from project initiation until all requirements have been implemented and validated. D is the most tempting distractor: the **Business Analyst (BA)**, a member of the **Project Core Team (PCT)**, is precisely the 'more specialised role' the sentence anticipates and handles many requirements activities, but the default owner is the **PM**. The **Business Manager (BM)** (C) is only **Consulted** for tailoring and elaborating the artefact.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Requirements Management Plan, what is the role of the Project Core Team (PCT)?

options.A: Consulted
options.B: Responsible
options.C: Supports
options.D: Informed

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for the **Requirements Management Plan** reads AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=C, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=S, so the **Project Core Team (PCT)** is **Supports**. A is the trap: **Consulted** on this row belongs to the **Business Manager (BM)** and the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)**. This is the only one of the six Management Plans in Appendix B where the **PCT** is **S**.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Project Change Management Plan, what is the role of the Business Implementation Group (BIG)?

options.A: Supports
options.B: Informed
options.C: n.a.
options.D: Consulted

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for the **Project Change Management Plan** reads AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=I, so the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** is **Informed**. D is the most tempting distractor: the **BIG** is **Consulted** on the **Requirements**, **Issue**, **Quality** and **Communications Management Plans**, but is **Informed** on this plan and on the **Risk Management Plan**.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Risk Management Plan, what is the role of the Project Steering Committee (PSC)?

options.A: Consulted
options.B: Accountable
options.C: Informed
options.D: Supports

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for the **Risk Management Plan** reads AGB=I, PSC=C, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=I, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=I, so the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** is **Consulted**. C is the most tempting distractor: the **PSC** is **Informed** on four of the six Management Plans, so this plan and the **Quality Management Plan** (where the **PSC** is **Accountable**) are the two exceptions. **Accountable** here is the **Project Owner (PO)**, who approves the plan.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Quality Management Plan, which role is Accountable?

options.A: The Solution Provider (SP)
options.B: The Project Owner (PO)
options.C: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.D: The Project Quality Assurance (PQA)

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for the **Quality Management Plan** reads AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=C, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C, so the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** is **Accountable**. This matches step 15, which requires the planned activities and timetable to be presented to the **PSC** for approval. B is the trap: the **Project Owner (PO)** is **Accountable** for the other five Management Plans but is only **Consulted** here. The **PQA** (D) reviews project quality but carries no entry in this RAM.
changes: Explanation rewritten in English against the guide; answer key and page reference confirmed correct.

question: Which procedure is also documented in the Quality Management Plan?

options.A: The benefits realisation procedure
options.B: The procurement procedure
options.C: The configuration management procedure
options.D: The escalation procedure

explanation: The **Quality Management Plan** states that a **configuration management** procedure is also documented in it. Configuration management lets project teams handle project artefacts and deliverables effectively: correct versions delivered, unauthorised changes prevented, artefact traceability. That is why C is right. D is the tempting distractor: the **escalation procedure** is defined and tailored in the **Project Handbook** (p.44) and is only referenced by the management plans, which are told not to duplicate it.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Communications Management Plan, what is the role of the Business Manager (BM)?

options.A: Informed
options.B: Accountable
options.C: Consulted
options.D: Supports

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for the **Communications Management Plan** is AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=C. The **Business Manager (BM)** 'provides input and assists in its creation', which matches the **Supports (S)** definition: the role works with the responsible role and carries out part of the activity. C is the trap. **Consulted (C)** only contributes input or review, and that is what the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** and the **Project Core Team (PCT)** get on this row, not the BM.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: How does the Issue Management Plan define issues?

options.A: Unplanned project-related events that require a project management action
options.B: Requests to amend the agreed baseline of the project
options.C: Deviations detected during quality control activities
options.D: Uncertain events that may impact the project objectives

explanation: The **Issue Management Plan** defines issues as unplanned project-related events that require a project management action. D is the trap: an uncertain event that may impact the objectives is a **risk**, not an issue. B describes a **Change Request**, an appeal to amend the agreed baseline of the project (glossary, p.124), and C describes a quality control finding.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: In the Change Log, which status indicates that the change has been incorporated into some other change and is no longer being actively handled?

options.A: Merged
options.B: Rejected
options.C: Postponed
options.D: Implemented

explanation: In the **Change Log**, the status **Merged** indicates that the change has been merged into some other change, so it is no longer being actively handled; merging is common when there are many changes. D is the tempting distractor: **Implemented** means the work implementing the change has been incorporated into the **Project Work Plan**, not folded into another change. **Postponed** means postponed indefinitely and **Rejected** means the change was turned down.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: How is the Risk Level (RL) calculated in the Risk Log?

options.A: RL = Likelihood + Impact
options.B: RL = Impact ÷ Likelihood
options.C: RL = Likelihood × Impact
options.D: RL = (Likelihood + Impact) ÷ 2

explanation: The **Risk Log** defines the **Risk Level (RL)** as the product of the **Likelihood (L)** and the **Impact (I)**: **RL = L * I**. Each factor is scored from 5 (Very high) down to 1 (Very low), which gives the relative scale of 1 to 25 used by the **Risk Likelihood/Impact Matrix** (p.101). A is the trap: the two values are multiplied, not added; adding them would cap the scale at 10 and break the colour banding of the matrix.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: In the Risk Log, how should the risk description be structured?

options.A: As a simple one-line title
options.B: As a SWOT analysis
options.C: As a formulation in the form of Cause – Risk – Effect, along with potential risk inter-dependencies
options.D: As a list of corrective actions

explanation: The **Description** field of the **Risk Log** must contain a structured formulation of the opportunity or threat in the form **Cause - Risk - Effect**, along with potential risk inter-dependencies. A is wrong because the short one-line summary is the separate **Title** field of the log. B names a different technique entirely: **SWOT analysis** evaluates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats and is not a risk description format.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Which set of statuses is used in the Issue Log?

options.A: Proposed, Assessing, Waiting for Approval, Approved, Rejected, Closed
options.B: Submitted, Assessing, Waiting for approval, Approved, Rejected, Postponed, Merged, Implemented
options.C: Open, Postponed, Resolved, Closed
options.D: Identified, Analysed, Escalated, Accepted

explanation: The **Issue Log** uses exactly four statuses: **Open**, **Postponed**, **Resolved** and **Closed**. B is the trap: Submitted / Assessing / Waiting for approval / Approved / Rejected / Postponed / Merged / Implemented is the **Change Log** status list (p.96). A is the **Risk Log** list, which runs from Proposed to Closed (p.97), and D is not a PM² status set at all.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Which three numerical assessment fields does the Issue Log use?

options.A: Urgency, Impact and Size
options.B: Likelihood, Impact and Risk Level
options.C: Impact, Priority and Target date
options.D: Priority, Size and Escalation

explanation: The **Issue Log** scores each issue on three numerical fields: **Urgency**, **Impact** and **Size** (Size being the effort needed to resolve the issue), each from 5 (Very high) to 1 (Very low). B is the trap: **Likelihood**, **Impact** and **Risk Level** are **Risk Log** fields (p.97). D mixes the **Change Log** fields **Size** and **Priority** with **Escalation**, which is a Yes/No field, not a numerical score; the Issue Log has no Priority field.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Which field is specific to the Decision Log?

options.A: Likelihood
options.B: Risk response strategy
options.C: Target Delivery Date
options.D: People present

explanation: The **Decision Log** has a **People present** field: log the names of those present when the decision was made, with a reference to the relevant **Minutes of Meeting (MoM)** if appropriate. A and B are **Risk Log** fields (**Likelihood**, **Risk response Strategy**, p.97) and C is the **Change Log** field **Target Delivery Date** (p.96). Fields such as **Escalation**, Category and Traceability appear in several logs, so **People present** is the only one genuinely specific to the Decision Log.
changes: Answer key (D) and page 99 confirmed. Option D shortened to 'People present' so the four options are parallel in length and the correct answer is no longer flagged by being the longest. Explanation rewritten in English.

question: What does PESTEL stand for?

options.A: People, Economy, Strategy, Time, Environment and Leadership
options.B: Political, Ethical, Social, Technical, Economic and Legal
options.C: Planning, Executing, Scope, Time, Effort and Learning
options.D: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal

explanation: **PESTEL** stands for **Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal**. The analysis identifies the external factors that influence an organisation and could affect the objectives, planning or execution of projects, which makes it particularly useful for business justification and risk management. B is the trap: it swaps in 'Ethical' for Environmental and 'Technical' for Technological, so it is not the PM² acronym.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: What is the difference between a Deliverables Breakdown Structure (DBS) and a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)?

options.A: The DBS is used only in agile projects; the WBS only in waterfall projects
options.B: They are two names for the same technique
options.C: The DBS defines what the project will produce (as a whole and as parts); the WBS defines the work needed to produce them
options.D: The DBS defines the work needed; the WBS defines what the project will produce

explanation: The guide states it directly: the **Deliverables Breakdown Structure (DBS)** defines what the project will produce (as a whole and as parts), and the **Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)** defines the work needed to produce them. The DBS is an essential part of **Product Based Planning** and can precede the WBS, whose tasks and activities deliver those outputs. D is the same sentence with the two structures swapped, which is the most tempting wrong answer; A is wrong because neither technique is tied to an agile or waterfall approach.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: What does the critical path represent?

options.A: The sequence of activities with the greatest number of resources
options.B: The set of activities with the highest risk level
options.C: The path with the highest cost in the project
options.D: The longest necessary path of planned activities, which also represents the shortest possible duration of the project to completion

explanation: The **Critical Path Method (CPM)** calculates the longest necessary path, that is the longest unavoidable duration, of planned activities from the beginning to the end of the project. Because the critical path represents the longest necessary path of activities, it also represents the shortest possible duration of the project to completion. A, B and C describe resource load, risk level and cost, none of which define the critical path: it is a duration concept only.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: In Earned Value Management (EVM), Earned Value is also known as which of the following?

options.A: Budgeted Cost of Work Performed (BCWP)
options.B: Estimate at Completion (EAC)
options.C: Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled (BCWS)
options.D: Actual Cost of Work Performed

explanation: In **Earned Value Management (EVM)** the principal metrics are the **Planned Value (PV)**, also known as **Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled (BCWS)**; the **Actual Cost (AC)**, also known as Actual Cost of Work Performed; and the **Earned Value (EV)**, also known as **Budgeted Cost of Work Performed (BCWP)**. D is the trap: Actual Cost of Work Performed is the alias of **AC**, not of EV; C is the alias of PV. **Estimate at Completion (EAC)** in B is a forecasting KPI derived from these metrics, alongside **SV/SPI**, **CV/CPI**, **ETC** and **TCPI**.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: What does the Pareto principle state, as applied in PM²?

options.A: 80% of the effects come from 20% of the causes
options.B: 80% of the budget is spent in the last 20% of the schedule
options.C: 50% of the risks generate 50% of the issues
options.D: 20% of the effects come from 80% of the causes

explanation: The **Pareto principle** states that generally 80% of the effects come from 20% of the causes, for example 80% of costs attributable to 20% of activities. **Pareto Analysis** applies this to risk or quality management so the team can focus on the top 20% of causes with the highest impact and prioritise mitigation or contingency actions. D is the classic trap: it reverses the two figures.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: In PM²-PgM, who is accountable for the programme's success?

options.A: The Programme Manager (PgM)
options.B: The Programme Business Manager (PgBM)
options.C: The Programme Steering Committee (PgSC)
options.D: The Programme Owner (PgO)

explanation: The **Programme Owner (PgO)** is accountable for the programme's success. A is the trap: the day-to-day management of the programme is delegated to the **Programme Manager (PgM)**, whose focus is to achieve the programme **outcomes**, so the PgM is responsible rather than accountable. The **Programme Business Manager (PgBM)** represents the PgO on a daily basis and focuses on realising the programme **benefits**.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Which roles comprise the Programme Steering Committee (PgSC)?

options.A: The Programme Owner (PgO) and the Project Owners (POs) of all component projects
options.B: The Programme Owner (PgO), the Programme Business Manager (PgBM) and the Programme Manager (PgM)
options.C: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) and the Programme Manager (PgM)
options.D: The Programme Manager (PgM) and the Programme Support Team (PgST)

explanation: The **Programme Steering Committee (PgSC)** comprises the **Programme Owner (PgO)**, the **Programme Business Manager (PgBM)** and the **Programme Manager (PgM)**, with other expert roles participating as needed; it is responsible for realising the programme's objectives and benefits. D is the trap: the **Programme Support Team (PgST)** is a temporary body that provides administrative assistance to the programme and its component projects (p.108) and is not part of the PgSC. A is wrong because component-project **Project Owners (POs)** are not listed as PgSC members.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Which of the following is one of the four groups of activities of the PM² Portfolio management process?

options.A: Portfolio Framework Definition
options.B: Portfolio Acceptance Management
options.C: Portfolio Outsourcing
options.D: Portfolio Transition Management

explanation: The **PM² Portfolio management** process is organised in four groups of activities: **Portfolio Framework Definition**, **Portfolio Composition**, **Portfolio Realisation**, and **Stakeholder Management & Communication**. A names the first of these, which delineates the portfolio structure, the governance bodies and their responsibilities together with the necessary processes. D is the trap: **Manage Transition** is a PM² project-level Monitor & Control activity, not a portfolio activity group; the same applies to deliverables acceptance (B) and outsourcing (C).
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Which set of principles does the guide list as the fundamental Data Protection principles under the GDPR?

options.A: Lawfulness, Fairness and Transparency, Accuracy, Purpose Limitation, Data Minimization, Storage Limitation, and Data Security including Integrity and Confidentiality
options.B: Prudence, Judgment and Insightfulness
options.C: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability
options.D: Independence, Impartiality, Objectivity and Loyalty

explanation: The guide lists the fundamental **Data Protection** principles under the **GDPR** as Lawfulness, Fairness and Transparency, Accuracy, Purpose Limitation, Data Minimization, Storage Limitation, and Data Security including Integrity and Confidentiality. C is the trap: confidentiality, integrity and availability are the three dimensions of **IT security** (p.111), not the GDPR principles. D lists the principles of the **PM² Code of Professional Conduct** (p.118) and B the intellectual virtues of Appendix F (p.119).
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: In the PM² Code of Professional Conduct, which principle means that 'staff members should be unbiased in any decisions they are called upon to make'?

options.A: Objectivity
options.B: Loyalty
options.C: Independence
options.D: Impartiality

explanation: In the **PM² Code of Professional Conduct**, **IMPARTIALITY** means that staff members should be unbiased in any decisions they are called upon to make. A is the near-miss: **OBJECTIVITY** requires that conclusions drawn as part of the project work be balanced and based on a thorough analysis of the facts and legal background, so it is about the reasoning, not about being unbiased in decisions. **INDEPENDENCE** is about serving the common good free of private or political interests, and **LOYALTY** is loyalty towards the organisation.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: According to Appendix F, the virtue of courage is described as the productive mean between which two extremes?

options.A: Meekness and vanity
options.B: Boorishness and buffoonery
options.C: Cowardice (deficiency) and audacity or fearlessness (excess)
options.D: Stinginess and wastefulness

explanation: Appendix F describes the virtue of **courage** as the management of risk taking and as the productive mean between cowardice (a deficiency) and audacity or fearlessness (an excess). D is the tempting distractor: stinginess and wastefulness are the two extremes of **generosity**, also on p.119. A gives the extremes of **magnanimity** and B those of **humour**, both defined on p.120.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: According to the glossary, renaming a section of an artefact or defining a risk as major when its impact is medium or higher is an example of which of the following?

options.A: Tailoring
options.B: Change control
options.C: Configuration management
options.D: Customisation

explanation: The glossary defines **Customisation** of the PM² Methodology as defining specific project management parameters to address the project's particularities, usually thresholds, scales and other parameters (for example defining a risk as major when its impact is medium or higher), plus any minor changes to the artefacts such as renaming a section. A is the trap that the glossary itself flags: changes to the methodology are not customisations but **Tailoring**, which adapts one or more of the four pillars, such as changing the governance, adding or removing process steps or artefact sections, or adding stages to a phase (p.139). C is wrong because **configuration management** controls the project's assets and versions, it does not set parameters.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: According to the glossary, what would happen without tolerances?

options.A: Risk levels could not be calculated
options.B: Every issue would be escalated immediately, and the Project Steering Committee (PSC) would end up running the project
options.C: The project would have no baselines
options.D: The Project Manager (PM) could not produce Project Reports

explanation: The glossary defines **Tolerance** as the allowable deviation above or below a target for time, cost or other project variables such as quality, scope and risk; once the deviation passes the agreed threshold, the current management level escalates to a higher level. It then states explicitly that without tolerance every issue would be escalated immediately and the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** would end up running the project. C is the trap: **baselines** are agreed reference values changed through the change management process and exist independently of tolerances.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: According to the glossary, which roles belong to the Provider Side?

options.A: The Solution Provider (SP), the Project Manager (PM) and the Project Core Team (PCT)
options.B: The contractors and their Contractor's Project Manager (CPM)
options.C: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) and the Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.D: The Project Owner (PO), the Business Manager (BM) and the Business Implementation Group (BIG)

explanation: The glossary defines the **Provider Side** as the resources of the project that develop and implement the solution: the **Solution Provider (SP)**, the **Project Manager (PM)** and the **Project Core Team (PCT)**. D is the trap: the **Project Owner (PO)**, the **Business Manager (BM)** and the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** are the **Requestor Side**, also called the Client Side. B is wrong because in PM² the provider is internal to the organisation and different from any external contractors, who are led by the **Contractor's Project Manager (CPM)**.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: According to the glossary, what is the key difference between success criteria and benefits?

options.A: Success criteria are defined by the contractor, benefits by the Project Owner (PO)
options.B: Success criteria are qualitative only, benefits are quantitative only
options.C: There is no difference; the terms are synonyms
options.D: Success criteria can be measured at project closure, while benefits are often achieved long after project closure

explanation: The glossary warns directly against confusing the two: **success criteria** can be measured at project closure, whereas **benefits** are often achieved long after project closure. B is the trap: success criteria comprise the standards by which the project is judged, they can be qualitative or quantitative and are ideally **SMART**, so the qualitative/quantitative split is not the distinction. C is wrong because the guide treats them as two clearly separate concepts, and A invents a role split the guide never makes.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Which of the following is listed as an input to the Business Implementation Plan?

options.A: The Project-End Report
options.B: The Transition Plan
options.C: The Deliverables Acceptance Note
options.D: The Outsourcing Plan

explanation: The inputs listed for the **Business Implementation Plan** are the **Business Case** and **Project Charter**, the **Project Handbook** and **Project Work Plan**, the **Transition Plan** and the **Quality Management Plan**. A is the trap: the **Project-End Report** is a Closing Phase output, not a Planning Phase input. Note the reciprocal link: the **Business Implementation Plan** is itself an input to the **Transition Plan** (p.51), so the two plans are interdependent.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Looking across the whole RASCI summary, for which two elements is the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) Accountable?

options.A: The Business Case and the Project Charter
options.B: The Outsourcing Plan and Manage Outsourcing
options.C: The Project Work Plan and Control Cost
options.D: The Transition Plan and Manage Transition

explanation: In the RAM (RASCI) summary tables the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** is **Accountable (A)** on exactly two rows: the **Outsourcing Plan** in Planning and **Manage Outsourcing** in Monitor & Control. On every other row the AGB is **Informed (I)**. D is the trap: for the **Transition Plan** and **Manage Transition** it is the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** that is Accountable, with the AGB only Informed. For the **Business Case** and the **Project Charter** in A, Accountable is the **Project Owner (PO)** and the **PSC** respectively.

question: In how many entries of the RASCI summary tables is the Business Manager (BM) Responsible (R)?

options.A: Only in the Business Case
options.B: In none of them
options.C: In four: the Project Initiation Request, the Business Case, the Business Implementation Plan and Manage Business Implementation
options.D: In all Planning Phase artefacts

explanation: In the RAM (RASCI) summary tables the **Business Manager (BM)** is **Responsible (R)** on four rows: the **Project Initiation Request**, the **Business Case**, the **Business Implementation Plan** and **Manage Business Implementation**. These are exactly the business-side items the **Project Manager (PM)** does not drive: on the last two the PM is only **Supports (S)** and on the Project Initiation Request the PM is n.a. D is the trap: on every other Planning Phase artefact the BM is **Supports** or **Consulted**, never Responsible.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Issue Management Plan, what is the role of the Project Core Team (PCT)?

options.A: Responsible
options.B: Supports
options.C: Consulted
options.D: Informed

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for the **Issue Management Plan** is AGB=I, PSC=I, PO=A, BM=C, BIG=C, SP=I, PM=R, PCT=C, so the **Project Core Team (PCT)** is **Consulted (C)**: it provides input and review but does not carry out part of the work. question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Project-End Report, what is the role of the Business Manager (BM)?

options.A: Responsible
options.B: Supports
options.C: Informed
options.D: Accountable

explanation: The RAM (RASCI) row for the **Project-End Report** is AGB=I, PSC=A, PO=C, BM=S, BIG=C, SP=C, PM=R, PCT=C, so the **Business Manager (BM)** is **Supports (S)**. A is the trap: **Responsible (R)** is the **Project Manager (PM)**, who writes the report, while **Accountable (A)** is the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)**, not the Project Owner. The first three Closing Phase activities, the **Project-End Review Meeting**, **Lessons Learned and Post-Project Recommendations** and the **Project-End Report**, all share this identical RASCI row.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: Across all the PM² RASCI summary tables, for which single activity is the Project Manager (PM) Accountable rather than Responsible?

options.A: Manage Quality
options.B: Quality Assurance
options.C: Project Coordination
options.D: Information Distribution

explanation: **Quality Assurance** in the **Executing Phase** is the only row in the RASCI summary tables where the **Project Manager (PM)** is **Accountable (A)**, with the **Project Core Team (PCT)** as **Responsible (R)**: the PM is accountable for carrying out all Quality Assurance activities while the PCT provides the evidence of adherence to the standards (p.58). A is the classic trap: on **Manage Quality** in **Monitor & Control** the **Solution Provider (SP)** is Accountable and the PM is Responsible. On **Project Coordination** and **Information Distribution** the PM is Responsible and the **Project Owner (PO)** is Accountable.
changes: Answer key and page reference confirmed against the guide; explanation rewritten in English.

question: According to Chapter 1, which of the following does this guide itself provide to its readers?

options.A: A common vocabulary (glossary), best practices, links to PM² resources and to other PM² models
options.B: A binding contract template, a procurement checklist and an approved supplier list for EU projects
options.C: A certification syllabus, an examination question bank and the official pass marks for PM² exams
options.D: A staffing plan, a budget ceiling and a mandatory reporting calendar for every EU-funded project

explanation: Chapter 1 states that this guide provides a common vocabulary (glossary) that makes it easier for project teams to communicate, **best practices** from which **Project Managers (PMs)** and teams choose what brings most value, links to **PM² resources** (online resources, **artefact** templates and examples), and an introduction to other PM² models such as **PM²-PgM** and **PM²-PfM**. A reproduces that list. C is the strongest distractor because PM² is indeed 'fully supported by a comprehensive training programme', but the guide never claims to supply a certification syllabus, a question bank or pass marks. Note the difference with what the **PM² Methodology** provides (governance structure, process guidelines, artefact templates and guidelines, mindsets).
changes: new item

question: The PM² Guide lists the ways in which PM² improves the effectiveness of project management. Which of the following is one of them?

options.A: Introducing monitor and control activities only during the Executing Phase of the project
options.B: Clarifying the expectations of those involved as early as possible in the project lifecycle
options.C: Replacing project documentation with informal communication among the project team members
options.D: Transferring responsibility for project planning from the Project Manager to the Steering Committee

explanation: The guide's list is: improving communication and the dissemination of information, clarifying expectations as early as possible in the project lifecycle, defining the project lifecycle (from **Initiating** to **Closing**), providing guidelines for project planning, introducing **Monitor & Control** activities, proposing management activities and outputs, and providing a link to agile practices. B is taken verbatim from that list. A is the strongest distractor: **Monitor & Control** is a genuine PM² item, but it runs throughout the whole lifecycle, not only in the **Executing Phase**. C contradicts the guide, which calls project documentation a key project management activity.
changes: new item
