question: According to the PM² Guide, what is the purpose of the Centre of Excellence in PM² (CoEPM²)?

options.A: To audit European Union-funded projects and grants and to certify each project's compliance with PM²
options.B: To act as the Appropriate Governance Body for every project run inside the European Commission
options.C: To give the Commission and EU Institutions high-quality project management infrastructure and support
options.D: To develop national project management standards on behalf of the European Union member states

explanation: The purpose of the **Centre of Excellence in PM² (CoEPM²)** is to provide the European Commission and European Union Institutions with high-quality project management infrastructure, support and consulting services. It also supports the methodology internally, coordinates an inter-institutional **Project Support Network (PSN)** and promotes wider adoption through the **Open PM² Initiative** and the Digital Europe Programme. A is the tempting distractor: improved monitor and control of EU-funded projects and grants is listed as a benefit of *opening* PM², not as an audit or certification role of the CoEPM². B confuses the CoEPM² with the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)**, which sits inside an individual project's governance.
changes: new item

question: A Project Manager in one EU Institution wants guidance on PM² and on project management tools and techniques more broadly, and wants to exchange best practices with peers in other Institutions. Which body is designed to provide this decentralised support?

options.A: The Project Support Office (PSO) set up inside the Project Manager's own directorate
options.B: The Project Steering Committee (PSC) of the Project Manager's current project
options.C: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) that approves the project's Business Case
options.D: The PM² Project Support Network (PSN) of Local Project Support Offices (LPSOs)

explanation: The **PM² Project Support Network (PSN)** is an EU-Institutions-wide network of **Local Project Support Offices (LPSOs)**, coordinated and supported by the **CoEPM²**, which aims to become a decentralised project management support network providing guidance on both the **PM² Methodology** and the effective use of project management tools and techniques more broadly. It promotes the exchange of knowledge and best practices, collects feedback to improve PM², and lets LPSOs support each other as a community. A is the strongest distractor: a **Project Support Office (PSO)** is an organisational body providing support services inside one organisation, not the inter-institutional network.
changes: new item

question: According to the PM² Guide, projects are best managed with a special temporary organisational structure in order to do which of the following?

options.A: Guarantee that the same core team will stay together to maintain the product after its delivery
options.B: Keep the organisation's day-to-day operations running while the deliverables are in use
options.C: Postpone the identification of project stakeholders until the deliverables are produced
options.D: Create a business justification for the investment and monitor and control the project daily

explanation: The guide explains that projects differ from normal day-to-day work and are best managed with a special temporary organisational structure in order to define the scope and deliverables, create a business justification for the investment, identify stakeholders and define a **Project Core Team (PCT)**, create the project plans, assign and coordinate work, monitor and control the project daily, and hand over the deliverables and administratively close the project. D combines two items from that list. B is the strongest distractor because it describes **operations** — the ongoing day-to-day activities of a permanent organisation — which is exactly what a project is *not*.
changes: new item

question: A project's scope objective has been achieved and all deliverables have been produced and accepted by the organisation that requested them. According to the PM² Guide, what completes a successful project ending?

options.A: The deliverables are handed over to the Project Support Office (PSO) for maintenance
options.B: The deliverables are handed over to the client and the project team is disbanded
options.C: The deliverables stay with the project team until the expected benefits have been measured
options.D: The deliverables are handed over to the contractor and the Business Case is re-approved

explanation: The guide states that a successful project ends when its scope objective has been achieved and all deliverables have been produced and accepted by the organisation or person that requested the project (the client); the deliverables are then handed over to the client and the project team is disbanded. B states exactly this. C is the strongest distractor, and it would keep the project alive indefinitely: the guide notes that project **outcomes** and **benefits** are often realised only *after* the project has closed. A wrongly casts the **Project Support Office (PSO)** as the receiver of the deliverables.
changes: new item

question: Six months after a document management project closed, the sponsor asks the former Project Manager why the promised productivity gains were not already visible at hand-over. What does the PM² Guide say about this?

options.A: Project outcomes and benefits are often realised only after the project has been closed
options.B: All benefits must be measured and signed off before the Closing Phase is allowed to start
options.C: Benefits are the deliverables themselves, so they exist as soon as hand-over is completed
options.D: Outcomes are produced by the project team during the Executing Phase as project outputs

explanation: PM² distinguishes **outputs** (deliverables), which introduce a change, from the **outcome** that results from the change, and from the **benefits**, which are the measurable improvements resulting from that outcome. The guide explicitly notes that project outcomes and benefits are often realised only after the project has closed, so A is correct. C is the strongest distractor: deliverables are described as merely a means to an end, never as the benefits themselves. B would make closure impossible for most projects.
changes: new item

question: How does the PM² Guide describe Project Management?

options.A: The coordinated management of a set of related projects and activities to achieve strategic benefits
options.B: The ongoing day-to-day activities undertaken by a permanent organisation to deliver its services
options.C: Planning, organising, securing, monitoring and managing the resources and work to deliver project goals
options.D: Grouping investments together to control financial resources and to identify organisational priorities

explanation: PM² describes **Project Management** as the activities of planning, organising, securing, monitoring and managing the resources and work necessary to deliver specific project goals and objectives in an effective and efficient way. C states this. A is the strongest distractor because it is the guide's description of **programme management**, where a **Programme Manager (PgM)** coordinates efforts between projects. B describes **operations** and D describes **project portfolio management**.
changes: new item

question: Which of the following is listed in the PM² Guide as a purpose of project documentation?

options.A: It replaces the phase gate reviews that are carried out at the end of each project phase
options.B: It guarantees the acceptance of the deliverables by the Project Owner (PO) at hand-over
options.C: It transfers accountability for the project scope from the client to the project team
options.D: It provides the information required by official audits and supports organisational memory

explanation: The guide lists what project documentation does: it sharpens thinking, crystallises planning, defines the scope for approval, gives stakeholders a clear picture of requirements, facilitates communication, provides a baseline for monitoring and controlling progress, records important decisions, provides the information required by official audits, and supports organisational memory as a historical reference. D pairs two of those items. A is the strongest distractor: documentation does provide a baseline for **Monitor & Control**, but the phase **review and approval gates** remain separate checkpoints that it cannot replace.
changes: new item

question: An organisation keeps only a basic permanent hierarchy; all work is organised and performed within temporary project organisations, and at the end of each project the resources are either reassigned to another project or returned to a resource pool. Which structure is this?

options.A: A weak matrix structure, in which the functional hierarchy keeps most of the authority
options.B: A projectized structure, in which resources work more or less exclusively for the project
options.C: A functional structure, in which project work is integrated into the permanent organisation
options.D: A balanced matrix structure, in which authority is shared with the permanent hierarchy

explanation: In a **projectized structure** there is only a basic permanent (functional) hierarchy and all work is organised and performed within temporary project organisations; resources are brought together specifically for the project, work more or less exclusively for it, and at the end are reassigned or returned to a resource pool. B matches the scenario. C is the strongest distractor and is the opposite case: in a **functional structure** project work is integrated into the work of the permanent organisation and members are borrowed from several sections, with the **Project Manager (PM)** holding limited authority.
changes: new item

question: A newly appointed Project Manager already knows PM² and has the technical competences to run the lifecycle. According to the PM² Guide, what else does the role require, and who else needs the same?

options.A: Only subject-specific knowledge, such as IT or policy, which the Project Support Office supplies
options.B: Knowledge of the business context, which the Project Owner is expected to hold on their behalf
options.C: The business context, organisational policies and post-delivery maintenance, as do Business Managers
options.D: Contract law and procurement rules, which are the sole responsibility of the Solution Provider

explanation: Beyond understanding the methodology and having the technical competences, the guide says **Project Managers (PMs)** also need to know how to communicate, lead, motivate and negotiate, plus the business context and general project environment, organisational policies and standards, and how the end-product or service will be maintained after it is delivered. It then adds that most, if not all, of these points are also required of **Business Managers (BMs)** — which is why C is correct. B is the strongest distractor: understanding the business context is required of the PM (and BM), not something delegated to the **Project Owner (PO)**. Subject-specific knowledge is called 'often relevant and useful', not the only extra requirement.
changes: new item

question: The PM² Guide gives one area a prominent position compared with all the other competences. Which one, and why?

options.A: Perspective competences, because strategy and governance determine the project's budget
options.B: Technical competences, because they decide whether the deliverables can be produced at all
options.C: People competences, because leadership and teamwork settle any conflict between the goals
options.D: Values and ethics, because our ethical profile guides how we apply all our other competences

explanation: The guide states that competences are not independent, and that the filter which determines what is more important (self or common interest, time or quality, results or balance) lies in our **values and ethics**. Competences related to the appreciation of values and ethics therefore have a prominent position compared to the rest, because it is our ethical profile that guides how we apply our competences and determines what is right or wrong in a given decision. C is the strongest distractor: **People Competences** is one of the two competence groups in the table, not the filter placed above them.
changes: new item

question: According to the PM² Guide, the virtues of judgment, prudence and insightfulness are comparatively more related to demonstrating which competences?

options.A: Perspective competences, such as strategy, governance and change and transformation
options.B: People competences, such as leadership, teamwork, negotiation and results orientation
options.C: Technical competences, such as scheduling, cost estimating and quality assurance work
options.D: Behavioural competences, such as personal communication and conflict and crisis management

explanation: The guide says that although all virtues (logical and moral) affect all competences, judgment, prudence and insightfulness are comparatively more related to demonstrating the **Perspective Competences**, while the moral virtues — honesty, fairness, friendliness, generosity, temperance, courage, humour, magnanimity and magnificence — are comparatively more related to the **People Competences** (see Appendix F). A is therefore correct and B is the strongest distractor, since it names the group linked to the *moral* virtues. C and D name groups that do not appear in the guide's two-column competence table.
changes: new item

question: According to the PM² Guide, on what basis does a project move on to the next phase of its lifecycle?

options.A: When the calendar date set for the phase in the baselined Project Work Plan is reached
options.B: When every activity of that phase type has permanently stopped being carried out
options.C: When the phase's goals are deemed achieved at a formal or less formal exit review
options.D: When the Project Manager judges that enough of the phase budget has been consumed

explanation: The **PM² lifecycle** has four sequential and non-overlapping phases, and a project moves on to the next phase when the goals of its current phase have been deemed achieved as the result of a formal (or less formal) **phase-exit review**. C states this rule. B is the strongest distractor: activities peak in their own phase but can still be executed in neighbouring phases — planning activities, for example, are repeated during the **Executing Phase** — so a phase does not end because a type of activity has stopped. Dates and budget consumption (A and D) do not authorise the transition.
changes: new item

question: An inexperienced team skips most of the definition work of the Initiating Phase and starts building deliverables straight away. According to the PM² Guide, what is the likely consequence?

options.A: The project will finish earlier, because effort peaks later during the Executing Phase
options.B: Outputs of poor quality and little value to end-users, a root cause of project failure
options.C: The phase gates will simply be merged, but the intended benefits will still be realised
options.D: The Project Steering Committee will take over the drafting of the Business Case itself

explanation: The guide warns that inexperienced project teams sometimes underestimate the importance of the work done in the initial project phases and start working on deliverables that are inadequately defined or planned; this delivers outputs of poor quality and little value to end-users, and is a common and costly mistake that is often the root cause of overall project failure and of the failure to realise the intended benefits. B says this. C is the strongest distractor because it assumes benefits survive weak definition, whereas the guide explicitly links this shortcut to benefits *not* being realised. It is precisely why adequate time must be invested in **Initiating** to define desired outcomes with a broad spectrum of stakeholders.
changes: new item

question: The Project Work Plan has been agreed, finalised, baselined and signed off, and the remaining Planning Phase artefacts are complete. What happens next according to the PM² Guide?

options.A: The Project Core Team (PCT) starts producing the deliverables, since the plan is baselined
options.B: The Project Owner (PO) approves the RfC gate and the Executing Kick-off Meeting is held
options.C: The Business Manager (BM) signs the Project Charter so that the Planning Phase can close
options.D: The Project Manager (PM) requests approval to move on to Executing and the PSC decides

explanation: Once agreed and finalised, the **Project Work Plan** is baselined and signed off; the **Project Manager (PM)** then uses the outputs of the **Planning Phase** to request approval to move on to the **Executing Phase**, and that decision is taken by the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)**. This is the **RfE (Ready for Executing)** gate. A is the strongest distractor: producing deliverables begins only after the gate approval and the Executing Kick-off Meeting, not because the plan has been baselined. B names the wrong gate — **RfC (Ready for Closing)** comes at the end of Executing.
changes: new item

question: A project's finished deliverables have been transferred into the care, custody and control of the Project Owner (PO). Which duty does the PM² Guide still assign to the Project Manager?

options.A: Measuring the benefits achieved and reporting them to the Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: Maintaining the delivered product and supporting its users during the warranty period
options.C: Ensuring project documents are correctly filed and archived and resources formally released
options.D: Re-baselining the Project Work Plan so that the remaining budget can be carried over

explanation: In the **Closing Phase**, the **Project Manager (PM)** ensures that the deliverables produced are accepted, that all project documents are correctly filed and archived, and that all resources used by the project are formally released; overall performance and **Lessons Learned** are captured in the **Project-End Report** and the project is closed administratively. C matches those duties. B is the strongest distractor: user support and maintenance of the delivered output belong to **operations**, which begins once the main products have been produced and accepted, not to the project's closing activities.
changes: new item

question: What is the purpose of the review and approval gate at the end of each PM² phase?

options.A: To ensure the project is reviewed by the appropriate people before it moves to the next phase
options.B: To allow the Project Manager (PM) to re-estimate the remaining effort and cost of the work
options.C: To give the Project Support Office (PSO) an opportunity to tailor the methodology used
options.D: To let the contractor confirm that all invoices raised during the phase have been settled

explanation: At the end of each phase the project passes through a review and approval gate, which ensures that the project is reviewed by the appropriate people — the **Project Manager (PM)**, the **Project Owner (PO)**, the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** or another delegated role — before it moves on; these checkpoints contribute to overall project management quality and let the project proceed in a more controlled way. The three gates are **RfP**, **RfE** and **RfC**. B is the strongest distractor: re-estimating is part of **Monitor & Control** and of planning work, not the stated purpose of the gate.
changes: new item

question: Which statement reflects one of the PM² Mindsets?

options.A: Projects exist to demonstrate that the methodology has been correctly applied by the team
options.B: Project management methodologies are there to serve projects, not the other way around
options.C: Following the approved plan matters more than the value the project finally delivers
options.D: Outputs matter more than outcomes once the deliverables have been accepted by the client

explanation: **PM² Mindset** 2 states that project teams remain mindful that project management methodologies are there to serve projects and not the other way around, which is why B is correct and A is its exact inversion. C is the strongest distractor: **Mindset** 4 commits teams to delivering project results with maximum value rather than just following plans. D contradicts **Mindset** 3, the outcomes orientation applied to all projects and project management activities.
changes: new item

question: PM² Mindset 7 asks project teams to balance in the most productive way the often-conflicting project management 'Ps'. Which set does the guide list?

options.A: People, process, product, procurement, portfolio, programme, planning, performance, policy, price
options.B: Product, process, plan, people, price, promotion, place, positioning, partnership, publicity
options.C: Purpose, process, product, precision, prudence, priority, patience, persistence, planning, pace
options.D: Product, purpose, process, plan, planet, people, pleasure/pain, participation, perception, politics

explanation: **Mindset** 7 asks teams to balance in the most productive way the often-conflicting project management 'Ps' of product, purpose, process, plan, planet, people, pleasure/pain, participation, perception and politics. D reproduces that list exactly. A is the strongest distractor because it mixes genuine PM² vocabulary — **portfolio**, **programme**, procurement — into a list the guide never gives. B is the classic marketing mix and C is an invented set of virtues.
changes: new item

question: In a project, the client group and the provider group blame each other every time a defect appears in a deliverable. Which PM² Infrequently Asked Question (IAQ) addresses this situation directly?

options.A: 'Is this a task for them or for us?' — make client and provider work as one team
options.B: 'Do we know what we are doing?' — develop a clear and shared vision for the project
options.C: 'Should I be involved?' — contribute from any position and help others to get involved
options.D: 'Have we improved?' — commit to ongoing self- and organisational improvement

explanation: The **IAQ** 'Is this a task for "them" or for "us"?' tips project teams to make sure that client and provider groups work as one team towards a common goal, because real teamwork really works, and to foster clear, effective and frequent communication. A is therefore the right fit for the scenario. C is the strongest distractor: 'Should I be involved?' is about contributing from any position and promoting the contributions of all stakeholders, not about dissolving a client/provider divide. B concerns a shared project vision and a holistic approach.
changes: new item

question: According to the PM² Guide, which challenges do Agile approaches meet as the size of the organisation applying them grows?

options.A: The impossibility of producing documentation and the complete loss of project governance
options.B: Coordination between Agile and non-Agile teams and compliance with governance and audit needs
options.C: The need to replace the four PM² phases with iterations and to abolish all the phase gates
options.D: A shortage of certified Agile coaches and the high cost of specialised Agile tooling licences

explanation: The guide states that Agile approaches meet various challenges which often grow with the size of the organisations in which they are applied: coordination between Agile and non-Agile teams, compliance with various organisational governance and audit requirements, and organisational architecture and interoperability constraints. B names two of these. A is the strongest distractor and overstates the point: PM² recognises the positive contribution of the Agile way of thinking, and never claims Agile makes documentation or governance impossible. C invents a change to the **PM² lifecycle** that the guide does not describe.
changes: new item

question: According to Chapter 4 of the PM² Guide, how many project teams are there, and which roles make up the team?

options.A: One team, made up of the roles defined in the Performing and Managing Layers only
options.B: One team, made up of the roles defined in the Performing, Managing and Directing Layers
options.C: Two teams, one made up of the requestor-side roles and one of the provider-side roles
options.D: Three separate teams, one for each of the Performing, Managing and Directing Layers

explanation: The guide states that there is only one project team, composed of the people assuming the roles defined in the **Performing**, **Managing** and **Directing** Layers, and that these people need to work together as a team. The strongest distractor is A, which stops at the **Managing Layer**: the **Project Owner (PO)** and **Solution Provider (SP)** sit in the **Directing Layer** and are part of the same single team. The **Business Governing Layer**, which determines the vision and strategy for the organisation as a whole, is not one of the three layers that make up the project team.
changes: new item

question: Which statement about the Steering Layer is correct?

options.A: It determines the vision and strategy for the organisation as a whole and consists of high-level management committees
options.B: It carries out the project work and consists of the Business Implementation Group (BIG) and Project Core Team (PCT)
options.C: It provides general project direction and guidance and consists of the Directing and Managing Layer roles plus optional roles
options.D: It focuses on the day-to-day management of the project and consists of the Business Manager (BM) and Project Manager (PM)

explanation: The guide defines the **Steering Layer** as providing general project direction and guidance, keeping the project focused on its objectives, and being composed of the roles defined in the **Directing** and **Managing** Layers plus other optional roles; it reports to the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)**. Option A describes the **Business Governing Layer**, B the **Performing Layer** and D the **Managing Layer**. D is the strongest distractor because the **BM** and **PM** are indeed part of the Steering Layer, but they are only half of it.
changes: new item

question: At a phase gate, a project's continued justification is challenged and the layer that owns the Business Case must defend it. Which layer champions the project and owns its Business Case?

options.A: The Business Governing Layer
options.B: The Managing Layer
options.C: The Steering Layer
options.D: The Directing Layer

explanation: The guide states that the **Directing Layer** champions the project and owns its **Business Case**, mobilises the necessary resources and monitors performance so the objectives are realised. The strongest distractor is C: the **Steering Layer** contains the Directing Layer roles, but the guide attributes Business Case ownership specifically to the Directing Layer, whose roles are the **Project Owner (PO)** and **Solution Provider (SP)**. The **Managing Layer** produces and maintains artefacts day to day but does not own the Business Case.
changes: new item

question: Which description of the reporting lines inside the PM² project organisation is correct?

options.A: Members of the Performing Layer report to the Managing Layer, and members of the Managing Layer report to the Directing Layer
options.B: Members of the Performing Layer report to the Directing Layer, and members of the Managing Layer report to the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)
options.C: Members of the Managing Layer report to the Performing Layer, and members of the Directing Layer report to the Managing Layer
options.D: Members of the Performing Layer report to the Managing Layer, and members of the Managing Layer report to the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)

explanation: Chapter 4 states that members of the **Managing Layer** report to the **Directing Layer**, and that members of the **Performing Layer** report to the **Managing Layer**. The Managing Layer comprises the **Business Manager (BM)** and **Project Manager (PM)**; the Performing Layer comprises the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** and the **Project Core Team (PCT)**. D is the strongest distractor because it gets the bottom of the chain right but sends the Managing Layer straight to the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)**, skipping the Directing Layer: the AGB is the body with the authority to approve a project and release its funding, and it is the **Steering Layer** that reports to it. C simply inverts the chain.
changes: new item

question: A proposed project has a documented need, but nobody has yet approved it, agreed its stated objective or released the funding required to implement it. Which body holds that authority?

options.A: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)
options.C: The Project Owner (PO)
options.D: The Solution Provider (SP)

explanation: The guide defines the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** as the entity responsible for strategic planning and portfolio management and, in project terms, as the body with the authority to approve a project, agree its stated objective and release the funding required to implement it. The strongest distractor is the **PSC**: it is the key decision-making body inside the project and approves key artefacts, but it does not authorise the project's existence or release its funding. The **PO** chairs the PSC and mobilises resources within the agreed budget, which is not the same as releasing the funding.
changes: new item

question: Which of the following is listed in the guide as a responsibility of the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)?

options.A: Authorises deviations and scope changes that have a high impact on the project
options.B: Approves key project artefacts such as the Project Charter and Project Work Plan
options.C: Coordinates the resolution of escalated project issues and conflicts
options.D: Optimises and manages portfolio resources and benefits for the organisation

explanation: The **AGB** responsibility list is portfolio-level: it defines the corporate and business domain strategy, agrees and implements a **portfolio management framework**, identifies, evaluates and authorises programmes and projects, monitors and controls **portfolio delivery performance**, and optimises and manages portfolio resources and benefits. A and B are **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** responsibilities, and C belongs to the **Project Owner (PO)**. A is the strongest distractor because both bodies authorise things, but high-impact deviations and scope changes are decided in the PSC.
changes: new item

question: An IT project must comply with the organisation's IT governance, data protection, information security and document management rules. According to the guide, which body is responsible for ensuring the project's adherence to those policies and rules?

options.A: The Project Core Team (PCT)
options.B: The Project Support Team (PST)
options.C: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.D: The Business Implementation Group (BIG)

explanation: One of the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** responsibilities is to ensure adherence to the organisation's policies and rules, with IT governance, data protection, information security and document management given as the examples. The strongest distractor is the **PST**, which can be extended with representatives from Legal, Procurement or Data Protection and manages project documentation; providing that support does not make it the responsible body. Specialists such as the **DPC** and **LISO** may sit in the PSC to advise, but responsibility for adherence stays with the PSC.
changes: new item

question: A change request with a high impact on the project's scope splits the team and no agreement can be reached. Who authorises such a deviation and has the final say on the decision?

options.A: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)
options.C: The Project Manager (PM)
options.D: The Business Manager (BM)

explanation: The guide states that the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** authorises deviations and scope changes with a high project impact and has the final say on decisions; it is also the body that deals with escalated issues and conflicts. The strongest distractor is the **AGB**, which authorises the project and its funding at portfolio level, but within the project the final say belongs to the PSC. The **PM** escalates unresolvable issues to the PSC rather than deciding them.
changes: new item

question: A project will process personal data about staff, and the Project Steering Committee (PSC) wants a specialist on the committee to consult and advise on data protection issues. Which optional PSC role fits that description?

options.A: The Document Management Officer (DMO)
options.B: The Local Information Security Officer (LISO)
options.C: The Data Protection Coordinator (DPC)
options.D: The Project Quality Assurance (PQA)

explanation: In the table of indicative optional **PSC** members, the **Data Protection Coordinator (DPC)** is the role that consults and advises on data protection issues. The strongest distractor is the **LISO**, who consults and advises on security issues, which is a related but different remit. The **DMO** ensures the coherent implementation of document management roles, and the **PQA** is responsible for quality assurance and auditing.
changes: new item

question: Which role does the PM² Guide describe as 'the client of the project'?

options.A: The User Representative (UR)
options.B: The Project Owner (PO)
options.C: The Business Manager (BM)
options.D: The Solution Provider (SP)

explanation: The guide opens the **Project Owner (PO)** section with the statement that the PO is the client of the project and, as such, sets the business objectives and ensures that project outcomes are in line with business objectives and priorities. The strongest distractor is the **BM**, who represents the PO on a daily basis within the project but is not the client. The **UR** represents the interests of end users, and the **SP** is the key Directing Layer role on the provider side.
changes: new item

question: Business risks are materialising on a project and extra business-side resources are needed within the approved budget. Which role owns the business risks and mobilises the resources necessary for the project in accordance with the agreed budget?

options.A: The Business Manager (BM)
options.B: The Project Manager (PM)
options.C: The Solution Provider (SP)
options.D: The Project Owner (PO)

explanation: Two **Project Owner (PO)** responsibilities apply here: the PO owns the **business risks** and ensures outcomes stay in line with business objectives, and the PO mobilises the resources necessary for the project in accordance with the agreed budget. The strongest distractor is the **PM**, who performs risk management activities for project-related risks, not business risks. The **SP** mobilises the required resources from the provider side only, and the **BM** ensures business resources are made available but does not own the business risks.
changes: new item

question: A contractor's team is underperforming on an outsourced work package whose objectives were approved at the outset. Which role is accountable for the contractor's performance?

options.A: The Contractor's Project Manager (CPM)
options.B: The Solution Provider (SP)
options.C: The Project Manager (PM)
options.D: The Project Owner (PO)

explanation: The **Solution Provider (SP)** approves the objectives of any outsourced activities and deliverables and, in doing so, becomes accountable for the contractor's performance. The strongest distractor is the **CPM**, who leads the contractor's staff and plans, controls and reports on the production of outsourced deliverables, but accountability towards the project remains with the SP. The **PM** coordinates the **PCT** and works closely with the CPM, while the **PO** is accountable for the project's overall success, not specifically for the contractor.
changes: new item

question: User training must be scheduled and delivered and the business organisation must be ready to accommodate the deliverables when the Solution Provider (SP) makes them available. Which role represents the Project Owner (PO) on a daily basis and handles this?

options.A: The Business Manager (BM)
options.B: The User Representatives (URs)
options.C: The Project Manager (PM)
options.D: The Business Implementation Group (BIG)

explanation: The guide states that the **Business Manager (BM)** represents the **PO** on a daily basis within the project, and lists among the BM's responsibilities ensuring that the business organisation is ready to accommodate the deliverables, leading the implementation of business changes within the user community and coordinating the schedule and delivery of any user training. The strongest distractor is the **BIG**: it prepares the affected business area and advises on readiness for change, but it is coordinated by the BM and does not represent the PO. The **PM** runs the project side, not the business change.
changes: new item

question: Which set of duties does the guide assign to the Project Manager (PM)?

options.A: Chairing the Project Steering Committee (PSC), coordinating escalated issues and accepting the Business Case
options.B: Coordinating the Business Implementation Group (BIG), leading the business change and coordinating user training
options.C: Liaising between the Directing and Performing Layers and reporting to the PSC at regular predefined intervals
options.D: Assuming overall accountability for the deliverables, mobilising provider-side resources and approving outsourced objectives

explanation: The **Project Manager (PM)** oversees the project on a daily basis; the responsibility list ends with monitoring project status and reporting to the **PSC** on progress at regular predefined intervals, escalating unresolvable project issues to the PSC, and liaising between the **Directing** and **Performing** Layers. A lists **Project Owner (PO)** duties, B lists **Business Manager (BM)** duties and D lists **Solution Provider (SP)** duties. B is the strongest distractor because the PM works very closely with the BM, but the client-side coordination and business change belong to the BM.
changes: new item

question: How does the guide describe the composition of the Business Implementation Group (BIG)?

options.A: The specialist roles that create the deliverables, coordinated by the Project Manager (PM)
options.B: Business and user group representatives on the requestor side, coordinated by the Business Manager (BM)
options.C: Representatives of various horizontal services and units, coordinated by the Project Support Office (PSO)
options.D: A balanced mix of requestor- and provider-side representatives, chaired by the Project Owner (PO)

explanation: The guide places the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** on the requestor side, made up of representatives of business and user groups and coordinated by the **Business Manager (BM)**; it plans and implements the business changes needed to integrate the deliverables into everyday work. A describes the **Project Core Team (PCT)**, C the **Project Support Team (PST)** and D the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)**. A is the strongest distractor because both groups sit in the **Performing Layer**, but the PCT is the provider-side team coordinated by the **PM**.
changes: new item

question: Before go-live, someone must perform the user acceptance tests, sign off the user-related documents and guarantee business stability during the transition towards the new operational state. Which role does the guide make responsible for this?

options.A: The Project Core Team (PCT)
options.B: The Business Manager (BM)
options.C: The Project Quality Assurance (PQA)
options.D: The User Representatives (URs)

explanation: The **User Representatives (URs)** responsibility list includes performing user acceptance tests, signing off on user-related documents such as the requirements document and deliverable acceptance testing, and guaranteeing business stability during the transition towards the new operational state; the URs also communicate and prioritise user opinions in the **PSC**. The strongest distractor is the **BM**, who ensures the delivered products fulfil the users' needs and coordinates the client side, but the guide assigns the acceptance testing and sign-off to the URs. The **PQA** reviews processes and artefacts against quality standards, which is a different check.
changes: new item

question: In which meeting does the Project Core Team (PCT) participate during the collection of Lessons Learned?

options.A: The Planning Kick-off Meeting
options.B: The Executing Kick-off Meeting
options.C: The Project-End Review Meeting
options.D: A Project Steering Committee (PSC) meeting

explanation: The last responsibility listed for the **Project Core Team (PCT)** is that it participates in the **Project-End Review Meeting** during the collection of **Lessons Learned**. The strongest distractor is D: the PCT does participate in project meetings as needed and helps resolve issues, but the PSC is the decision-making body, not where the team's lessons learned are collected. The kick-off meetings in A and B open the Planning and Executing Phases and therefore precede any lessons learned collection.
changes: new item

question: On a large project, the Project Manager (PM) delegates a range of coordination and supportive tasks to a Project Management Assistant (PMA), who also acts as the PM's backup in meetings. What does the guide say about responsibility in this arrangement?

options.A: The Project Manager (PM) remains responsible for all project management tasks and deliverables
options.B: Responsibility for the delegated tasks passes to the Project Management Assistant (PMA)
options.C: The Project Management Assistant (PMA) becomes accountable to the PSC for those tasks
options.D: Responsibility for the delegated tasks is shared equally between the PM and the PMA

explanation: The guide allows the **PM** on large projects to delegate management tasks to a **Project Management Assistant (PMA)**, who can act as the PM's backup in meetings, but it states explicitly that the PM remains the person responsible for all project management tasks and deliverables. The strongest distractor is B, which confuses delegation of work with transfer of responsibility. The PMA may also be part of a **Project Support Team (PST)** assigned to the project, but that does not change who is responsible.
changes: new item

question: Which of the following is listed as a responsibility of the Project Support Team (PST)?

options.A: Reviews the project's processes and artefacts, identifies non-conformities and recommends corrective actions
options.B: Administers Project Steering Committee (PSC) meetings and manages documentation versioning and archiving
options.C: Analyses the impact of the project's implementation on business processes, staff and organisational culture
options.D: Approves the objectives of outsourced deliverables and reports on the progress of subcontracted activities

explanation: The **Project Support Team (PST)** provides administrative support, defines requirements for reporting and communication, administers **PSC** meetings and drafts the related reports, supports the **PM** in planning, monitoring and controlling, advises on tools, and manages project documentation including versioning and archiving. A describes the **Project Quality Assurance (PQA)**, C the **Business Implementation Group (BIG)** and D the **Solution Provider (SP)** and **CPM**. A is the strongest distractor because both are support-type roles, but the PQA works independently of the PM on quality.
changes: new item

question: An independent check of a project finds that several artefacts do not conform to the set quality standards and corrective actions must be recommended. Which role carries out this work, independently of the Project Manager (PM)?

options.A: The Project Support Office (PSO)
options.B: The Project Support Team (PST)
options.C: The Document Management Officer (DMO)
options.D: The Project Quality Assurance (PQA)

explanation: The **Project Quality Assurance (PQA)** works independently of the **PM** and ensures the high quality of the project and its deliverables by reviewing processes and artefacts, identifying non-conformities with the set quality standards and recommending corrective actions; it may be a group or an individual staff member. The strongest distractor is the **PSO**, also called Project Management Office or Project Office, which is an optional structure providing services such as methodology application, information systems, governance and logistics rather than quality auditing. The **PST** gives administrative support and the **DMO** covers document management.
changes: new item

question: Which statement about the Responsibility Assignment Matrix (RAM) is correct?

options.A: It clarifies the roles and responsibilities for a given activity, with just one Responsible and one Accountable person per task
options.B: It records all the stakeholders of a given activity, allowing several Responsible and several Accountable people per task
options.C: It documents the escalation path for a given activity, with one Accountable person and no Responsible person per task
options.D: It presents the planned schedule of a given activity, with one Responsible person and several Accountable people per task

explanation: The guide defines the **RAM**, also known as the **RASCI** table, as a way of representing and clarifying the roles and responsibilities for a given activity, and states for both **Responsible** and **Accountable** that there is just one such person for any given task. B is the strongest distractor because teams often do spread work across several people, but the matrix records only one Responsible and one Accountable, with the others carrying **Supports (S)**. The RAM is not a schedule or an escalation path.
changes: new item

question: In a PM² RAM (RASCI) table, what distinguishes the Supports role from the Consulted role?

options.A: Supports (S) is kept informed of progress, while Consulted (C) works alongside the responsible person
options.B: Supports (S) gives an opinion on the task, while Consulted (C) is answerable for its correct completion
options.C: Supports (S) approves the completed task, while Consulted (C) carries out the work with the responsible person
options.D: Supports (S) helps complete the task, while Consulted (C) gives an opinion but does not help complete it

explanation: The guide says that roles with a **Supports (S)** function work with the person responsible and help complete the task, whereas **Consulted (C)** roles are those whose opinions are requested, with two-way communication, and the guide adds explicitly that the consulted role does not help complete the task. A and C invert the two definitions, and B mixes Consulted up with **Accountable (A)**, which is ultimately answerable for correct and thorough completion. In the guide's Business Case example, the **SP** and **PM** are Supports while the **PSC** and **URs** are Consulted.
changes: new item

question: According to the PM² Guide, which information does the Project Initiation Request contain?

options.A: The estimated effort and cost, the timeframe for completion and the type of delivery
options.B: A SWOT analysis of several candidate solutions and a detailed cost-benefit analysis
options.C: The work packages, the effort estimate per task and the overall project schedule
options.D: The conflict resolution procedure, the escalation path and the project mindsets

explanation: The guide states that the **Project Initiation Request** contains basic information on the estimated effort and cost, the timeframe for completion and the type of delivery, plus the expected impact, the success criteria, the project's relevance to the organisation's strategic direction and the key assumptions, constraints and risks. A reproduces that list. B is the strongest distractor because a **SWOT Analysis** of several solutions and a cost-benefit analysis are explicitly the content of the **Business Case**, not of the request. The guide also warns to keep the request to high-level information only, which rules out the work-package detail in C.
changes: new item

question: A Project Initiation Request has been drafted for a small project, and the organisation's approval process does not require corporate-level scrutiny at this size. Who can accept it and authorise work on a more elaborate Business Case?

options.A: The Business Manager (BM), who usually drafts the request on the Owner's behalf
options.B: The Project Owner (PO), who can accept it informally without a governance body
options.C: The Project Steering Committee (PSC), which must be convened before any approval
options.D: The Solution Provider (SP), as the unit that will carry out the project work

explanation: The guide's guideline "know your audience" says that, depending on the project size and the organisation's approval process, approval of the **Project Initiation Request** can be informal (the **Project Owner (PO)** accepts it) or formal (an **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** reviews and approves it), and the Approver row names exactly those two roles as able to accept the request and authorise work on a more elaborate **Business Case**. For a small project with no corporate scrutiny, the **PO** accepts it. A is the tempting distractor: the **PO** often delegates the drafting of the request to the **Business Manager (BM)**, but drafting is not approving — in the RAM (RASCI) the **BM** is Responsible and the **PO** is Accountable (A/S). C fails because the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** is not one of the named approvers of the request and is marked "n.a." for this artefact in the RASCI, and because approval need not be formal at all.
changes: new item

question: When does the lifecycle of the Project Initiation Request end?

options.A: When the Project Manager (PM) and the Project Core Team (PCT) are assigned
options.B: When the project passes the RfP (Ready for Planning) phase gate approval
options.C: When the Business Case and the Project Charter have both been created
options.D: When the Project Handbook is baselined during the Planning Phase

explanation: The guide states that the lifecycle of the **Project Initiation Request** ends with the creation of the **Business Case** and **Project Charter**: all its information is copied over, updated and further elaborated in those two documents, which remain "live" until the end of the project. B is the strongest distractor, but the **RfP** gate comes later and approves the **Business Case** and **Charter** — by then the request has already been superseded. Assignment of the **PM** and **PCT** (A) is a step within the initiation sequence, not the end of the request's life.
changes: new item

question: According to the Business Case key participants, who creates the Business Case and who supports them?

options.A: The Project Owner (PO), supported by the Business Manager (BM) and User Representatives (URs)
options.B: The Project Manager (PM), supported by the Project Core Team (PCT) and Support Office (PSO)
options.C: The Solution Provider (SP), supported by the Project Owner (PO) and the Business Implementation Group
options.D: The Business Manager (BM), supported by the Solution Provider (SP) and the Project Manager (PM)

explanation: The guide's key participants table for the **Business Case** says the **Business Manager (BM)** creates it, supported by the **Solution Provider (SP)** and the **Project Manager (PM)** (if known), while the approver is a preliminary **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** or a higher-level **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)**. A is the strongest distractor because the **Project Owner (PO)** is indeed named for the **Business Case** — but as Accountable, not as its author. The **PM** is often not even assigned yet, which also rules out B.
changes: new item

question: A project is being carried out under contract, as the result of a bid award. According to the Business Case guidelines, on what should its Business Case be based?

options.A: On the Project Charter and the Project Handbook agreed with the client at kick-off
options.B: On the Request for Proposal, the response to that request, and the contract itself
options.C: On the Project Initiation Request alone, since the contract already fixes the scope
options.D: On the Outsourcing Plan and the organisational procurement rules and procedures

explanation: The guide's guidelines state that, for projects carried out under contract (e.g. as a result of a bid award), the **Business Case** is created on the basis of the **Request for Proposal**, the response to that request, and the contract itself. C is the strongest distractor: the **Project Initiation Request** is indeed the normal input to the **Business Case**, but the contract-project guideline overrides that default. Note the other guidelines here too — the form and depth of the analysis depend on the level of investment, several solutions are considered with one recommended, and measurable success criteria must be identified.
changes: new item

question: While drafting the Project Charter, the Project Manager is handed a long list of detailed functional requirements by a User Representative. According to the guidelines, what should the Project Manager do?

options.A: Insert the full list into the Charter so that its approval covers the agreed scope
options.B: Move the detailed list into the Business Case, which justifies the investment
options.C: Present high-level needs and features, with the detail in a Requirements Document
options.D: Postpone the Charter until the detailed requirements are validated by the PSC

explanation: The **Project Charter** defines the project's objectives (scope, time, cost, quality), high-level requirements, risks, constraints, milestones and deliverables, and provides the baseline against which progress is measured. The guidelines say it should be brief and that detailed requirements should be avoided: they belong in another artefact such as a **Requirements Document**, or in an appendix to the **Charter** to be elaborated during planning. A is the tempting distractor because the **Charter** is part of the approval package, but stuffing it with detail defeats the guideline that stakeholders must be able to review it quickly.
changes: new item

question: The main project stakeholders have just finished reviewing the Project Charter. According to the steps in the guide, what happens next?

options.A: The Project Manager (PM) baselines the Charter and calls the Planning Kick-off Meeting
options.B: The Project Steering Committee (PSC) accepts it and the Project Owner (PO) may send it on
options.C: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) accepts it and the Business Case is then drafted
options.D: The Business Manager (BM) accepts it and forwards it to the Solution Provider (SP) team

explanation: The **Project Charter** steps run: the main project stakeholders review the **Charter** and the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)** accepts it; then the **Project Owner (PO)** sends the **Business Case** and **Charter** to the appropriate decision-making body for additional approval if needed. C is the strongest distractor because the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** does provide corporate-level approval — but only after the **PSC** has accepted, and the **Business Case** is an input to the **Charter**, so it is drafted first, not afterwards.
changes: new item

question: At the RfP (Ready for Planning) phase gate, who assesses whether the project is ready to start the Planning Phase, and whose approval of the Business Case and Project Charter is sought?

options.A: The Business Manager (BM) assesses it; the Project Owner (PO) gives the approval
options.B: The Project Owner (PO) assesses it; the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) approves
options.C: The Project Manager (PM) assesses it; the Project Steering Committee (PSC) approves
options.D: The Solution Provider (SP) assesses it; the Project Core Team (PCT) gives approval

explanation: At the first phase gate, **RfP (Ready for Planning)**, the **Project Manager (PM)** assesses whether the project is ready to commence the **Planning Phase** and seeks approval of the **Business Case** and **Project Charter** from the **Project Steering Committee (PSC)**. B is the strongest distractor: the **Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)** may give corporate-level approval of those documents earlier, but the gate itself is a **PSC** decision. If the **Business Case** or **Charter** is not approved, the project goes directly to the **Closing Phase**.
changes: new item

question: How is the Phase Exit Review Checklist intended to be used at a PM² phase gate?

options.A: By the Project Steering Committee (PSC), as the formal minutes of its gate decision
options.B: By the Project Support Office (PSO), to audit every artefact produced in the phase
options.C: By the Project Owner (PO), instead of reviewing the specific goals of the phase
options.D: By the Project Manager (PM), to guide the assessment alongside the phase's goals

explanation: PM² provides a template **Phase Exit Review Checklist** for each phase that can be used by the **Project Manager (PM)** to guide the assessment, alongside a review of the phase's specific goals. C is the strongest distractor because it names a plausible governance role but gets two things wrong: the checklist belongs to the **PM**, and it complements rather than replaces the review of the phase's goals. It is an assessment aid, not the record of the **PSC**'s decision (A).
changes: new item

question: Which statement about attendance at the Planning Kick-off Meeting is correct?

options.A: The User Representatives (URs) attend only when the Project Owner (PO) asks them
options.B: The Project Manager Assistant (PMA) attends if that role is part of the project
options.C: The Business Implementation Group (BIG) participates only as an optional attendee
options.D: The Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) is listed as a required participant here

explanation: The guide lists the **Project Core Team (PCT)**, **Business Implementation Group (BIG)**, **User Representatives (URs)**, **Solution Provider (SP)**, **Project Owner (PO)** and **Business Manager (BM)** as required participants of the **Planning Kick-off Meeting**, with the **Project Manager Assistant (PMA)** and **Project Support Office (PSO)** required to attend if they are part of the project. C is the strongest distractor: the **BIG** is a required participant, not an optional one — only "other project roles or stakeholders" attend optionally. The **PM** organises the meeting.
changes: new item

question: The Project Manager is wrapping up the Planning Kick-off Meeting. Which statement about this meeting is correct?

options.A: The final set of required project plans is documented in the Project Handbook
options.B: The overall approach may be brainstormed beyond the limits set by the Charter
options.C: The project timeline is agreed and baselined by the Project Steering Committee
options.D: The Project Charter is walked through only if the Business Case was rejected

explanation: Among the steps during the **Planning Kick-off Meeting**, the participants discuss the project plans needed, and the guide states that the final set of required project plans will be documented in the **Project Handbook**. B is the strongest distractor because brainstorming really is encouraged when discussing the overall approach — but explicitly "within the limits set by the **Project Charter**", not beyond them. Walking the participants through the **Charter** so they understand the scope is a standard step of every kick-off, which rules out D.
changes: new item

question: After the Planning Kick-off Meeting, what does the guide require of the Minutes of Meeting (MoM)?

options.A: They go only to those who attended, and are then archived by the Project Support Office
options.B: They replace the Risk Log and Issue Log entries for the items raised at the meeting
options.C: They are approved by the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) before being distributed
options.D: They go to the stakeholders named in the Charter and summarise risks and decisions

explanation: After the meeting, the **Minutes of Meeting (MoM)** are distributed to the appropriate stakeholders as identified in the **Project Charter**, and must include a summary of the issues raised, risks identified, decisions taken and changes proposed. B is the strongest distractor: the guide states that those issues, risks, decisions and changes should *also* be recorded in the relevant logs, so the **MoM** supplements the **Risk Log** and **Issue Log** rather than replacing them. Distribution is not limited to attendees (A).
changes: new item

question: According to the Project Handbook guidelines, which statement is correct?

options.A: The Handbook is baselined at the RfE gate and then frozen for the rest of the project
options.B: All Project Management Plans should be considered part of the Project Handbook
options.C: The Handbook is superseded by the Project Work Plan once the Executing Phase starts
options.D: The Handbook is discarded at project end once the Project-End Report is written

explanation: The guidelines state that all **Project Management Plans** should be considered part of the **Project Handbook**, that the **Handbook** must be kept up to date throughout the life of the project, and that during the **Closing Phase** it is an important point of reference for the **Project-End Review Meeting** and should be properly archived. A is the strongest distractor: freezing the **Handbook** contradicts the "kept up to date" guideline. D contradicts the archiving guideline — the **Handbook** is archived, not discarded.
changes: new item

question: A project needs a new role that does not exist in the standard PM² Roles & Responsibilities, and it will also merge two standard roles. According to the guide, what must be done?

options.A: Request a formal waiver from the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB) beforehand
options.B: Keep the standard roles in the Handbook and record the changes in the Work Plan
options.C: Justify and document the deviations, describing the new role's responsibilities
options.D: Avoid the change, as PM² roles may not be tailored to a project's circumstances

explanation: The Project Roles & Responsibilities section of the **Project Handbook** states that any deviations from the standard PM² Roles & Responsibilities should be justified and documented, and any new roles defined with their responsibilities clearly described. D is the strongest distractor, but PM² is explicitly meant to be tailored — what it demands is justification and documentation, not abstention. On that basis the **Project Stakeholder Matrix** is then tailored and named people are assigned to all project roles, using preliminary information from the **Project Charter**.
changes: new item

question: As the work becomes clearer, the Project Manager finds that two team members lack skills the project needs. According to the Resource Needs guidance, what should happen?

options.A: The gap is logged as a project risk and resolved through the Outsourcing Plan
options.B: The skills are listed in the Project Work Plan and training added to the schedule
options.C: A change request is raised so the Project Steering Committee can approve hiring
options.D: The skills are recorded in the Handbook and a Training Plan may be annexed to it

explanation: The guide states that as the work to be done becomes clearer, the skills needed must be recorded in the **Project Handbook**, and a **Training Plan** can be annexed to the **Handbook** if personnel need training in missing skills. The same section describes the hiring process if more skilled people are needed, and formalises how resources will be released at the end of the project. B is the strongest distractor: training activities do end up in the **Project Work Plan**, but the skills themselves and the **Training Plan** belong to the **Handbook**.
changes: new item

question: Which statement about the Project Work Plan is correct?

options.A: It is baselined but also kept up to date with work that emerges during Executing
options.B: It is baselined at the RfE gate and any later change goes into the Handbook
options.C: It is drafted by the Project Support Office (PSO), which owns the scheduling
options.D: It is replaced by the Project Schedule once the Executing Phase has started

explanation: Once tasks are scheduled the **Project Work Plan** becomes the basis for monitoring progress and controlling the project, and the guide says it should be baselined but also kept up to date, capturing all project-related work identified during planning or emerging during executing (e.g. risks, issues, corrective actions). C is the strongest distractor: the **Project Support Office (PSO)** may provide technical advice, for instance on scheduling, but the **Project Manager (PM)** coordinates all activities in developing the plan, assisted by the **Project Core Team (PCT)**.
changes: new item

question: The Project Manager has broken the project down into deliverables and then into work packages. According to the guide, which components come next in the Work Breakdown?

options.A: Activities, and then the tasks that make them up
options.B: Milestones, and then the deliverables they close
options.C: Effort estimates, and then the cost estimates
options.D: Phases, and then the project-specific stages

explanation: The **Work Breakdown** section of the **Project Work Plan** breaks the project into smaller, more manageable components — deliverables, work packages, activities and tasks — over multiple levels, each with progressively more detailed deliverables and work. After work packages come activities and then tasks. C is the strongest distractor because estimating does follow the breakdown, but the **Effort & Cost Estimates** are a separate section of the **Project Work Plan**, not a level of the breakdown itself.
changes: new item

question: Which of the following is listed as an input to the Work Breakdown section of the Project Work Plan?

options.A: The Effort & Cost Estimates, together with the Project Schedule constraints
options.B: The Project Handbook, together with the Planning Kick-off Minutes of Meeting
options.C: The Project Requirements, together with the Business Case and Project Charter
options.D: The Deliverables Acceptance Plan, together with the Quality Management Plan

explanation: The inputs listed for the **Work Breakdown** are the **Business Case** and **Project Charter** plus the **Project Requirements**. A is the strongest distractor because it reverses the dependency: the **Effort & Cost Estimates** take the **Work Breakdown** as *their* input, and the **Project Schedule** in turn takes the **Project Charter**, the **Work Breakdown** and the estimates. In B neither element is an input to the breakdown — the **Planning Kick-off Minutes of Meeting (MoM)** is an input to the **Project Handbook** and the **Project Stakeholder Matrix**, while the **Project Handbook** is itself an input to plans such as the **Outsourcing Plan** and the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan**. D pairs two plans that appear together as inputs to **Manage Quality**, not to the Work Breakdown.
changes: new item

question: The team has estimated the effort for every task in the Work Breakdown, but the Project Manager still cannot put a cost on several of them. According to the guide, what makes a task's cost calculable?

options.A: Placing the task on the schedule with a start date and an end date
options.B: Approving the Business Case budget for the project as a whole
options.C: Agreeing the acceptance criteria that apply to the deliverable
options.D: Assigning the task to a resource, or to a resource profile

explanation: The **Effort & Cost Estimates** section estimates the effort needed for each task identified in the **Work Breakdown**, based on resource availability and capabilities; the guide states that after a task is assigned to a resource (or to a resource profile) it also becomes possible to calculate its cost. A is the strongest distractor, but scheduling comes afterwards — the estimates are an input to the creation of the **Project Schedule**, so dates cannot be a precondition for costing.
changes: new item

question: A Project Manager schedules the first months of the Executing Phase in full detail and leaves the later work at a coarser level, to be detailed as the project proceeds. Which statement about the Project Schedule is correct?

options.A: Detailed scheduling may be done upfront or developed progressively later
options.B: The Project Owner (PO) uses the schedule to authorise and accept the work
options.C: The schedule must be complete in full detail before the Planning Phase ends
options.D: The schedule is derived from the Outsourcing Plan and contractor timelines

explanation: The guide states that detailed scheduling can be done for the entire project upfront, or alternatively worked out in adequate detail only for some early parts of the **Executing Phase** and then progressively developed in full detail — so the approach described is legitimate and C is wrong. B is the strongest distractor: it is the **Project Manager (PM)**, not the **Project Owner (PO)**, who uses the **Project Schedule** to authorise, coordinate and accept project work and to monitor overall progress.
changes: new item

question: While preparing the Outsourcing Plan, the Project Manager is asked why the contractor evaluation criteria have to be listed in advance. What reason does the guide give?

options.A: So the contractor can be chosen without running any tendering process at all
options.B: So selection rests on pre-set criteria and no single person or group sways it
options.C: So the Project Steering Committee (PSC) can delegate the contract signature
options.D: So the evaluation can be repeated by the Appropriate Governance Body (AGB)

explanation: Step 3 of the **Outsourcing Plan** requires listing the evaluation criteria for contractors, which "ensures that a contractor is selected on the basis of pre-set criteria and that no single person or group influences the decision"; the criteria may include capability and previous experience in similar projects. A is the strongest distractor because the plan does identify the method by which products are obtained, including a tendering process — pre-set criteria support that process rather than removing it. Separate steps cover who may interface with contractors and who signs the contract, the constraints imposed by pre-existing agreements or preferred suppliers, and the documentation deliverables expected from contractors.
changes: new item

question: Which of the following must be defined in the Deliverables Acceptance Plan?

options.A: The detailed quality control techniques used to test each project deliverable
options.B: The full list of validated requirements against which the client will sign off
options.C: The process and timeline for dealing with non-acceptance or partial acceptance
options.D: The penalties applied to a contractor whose deliverable has been rejected

explanation: The steps of the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan** include defining the process and timeline for dealing with non-acceptance (or partial acceptance), and the level of formality of the acceptance process — for example whether a signed **Deliverables Acceptance Note** is required. A and B are the strongest distractors, but the guidelines explicitly warn against duplicating information held in the **Quality Management Plan** and the **Requirements Management Plan**. For outsourced work, the acceptance process is documented in the contract, and the **Deliverables Acceptance Checklist** is tailored to the acceptance activities defined.
changes: new item

question: A Transition Plan is being prepared for a system roll-out. Which of the following does the guide list among its steps?

options.A: The training needs of the people in the organisation affected by the change
options.B: The sources of resistance to the change and the attitudes of key stakeholders
options.C: The evaluation criteria for the contractors who will run the new system
options.D: What must be completed before the transition can start and before it can end

explanation: The **Transition Plan** steps include documenting what must be completed before the transition can start and finish, deciding whether the physical or virtual environments must change, communicating possible business interruptions to affected stakeholders in good time, defining operational support and maintenance needs, and planning a formal announcement of the start and end of the transition. A and B are the strongest distractors: training needs and sources of resistance are steps of the **Business Implementation Plan**. Note that all transition activities become part of the **Project Work Plan** and are scheduled and controlled with the rest of the project.
changes: new item

question: Some change-sustaining activities will have to be carried out by the organisation after the project has closed. According to the guide, where are these identified?

options.A: In the Business Implementation Plan, possibly as future or follow-up projects
options.B: In the Transition Plan, as prerequisites for completing the transition period
options.C: In the Project-End Report, as the lessons learned from the Executing Phase
options.D: In the Project Handbook, as part of the selected delivery approach chosen

explanation: The final step of the **Business Implementation Plan** is to identify the change implementation and change-sustaining activities to be carried out by the organisation after the project ends, possibly as future or follow-up projects. B is the strongest distractor: the **Transition Plan** covers moving from the pre-project to the post-project state and stops at the end of the transition, whereas sustaining the change is a business implementation concern. Depending on the organisation, the business implementation activities can even be performed as a separate project.
changes: new item

question: A project has a Project Manager Assistant (PMA) and is supported by a Project Support Office (PSO). What does the PM² Guide say about their attendance at the Executing Kick-off Meeting?

options.A: Both may attend optionally, as the project's needs dictate
options.B: Only the Project Manager Assistant (PMA) is required to attend
options.C: Both are required to attend, as they are part of the project
options.D: Only the Project Support Office (PSO) is required to attend

explanation: The **Executing Kick-off Meeting** participants table lists the **Project Manager Assistant (PMA)** and the **Project Support Office (PSO)** as required to attend if they are part of the project. Both roles exist on this project, so both must be there, which makes C correct. A is the strongest distractor, but optional participation is what the guide reserves for other project roles or stakeholders, not for the **PMA** and **PSO**. The **Project Core Team (PCT)** is also a required participant, and the **Project Manager (PM)** organises the meeting.
changes: new item

question: During the Executing Kick-off Meeting, how does the PM² Guide treat the conflict resolution process and the escalation procedure?

options.A: The escalation procedure is agreed and the conflict resolution process is presented
options.B: The conflict resolution process is agreed and the escalation procedure is presented
options.C: Both are presented for information only, and neither is agreed at the meeting
options.D: Both are agreed at the meeting and then written into the Project Handbook

explanation: Step 4 of the during-the-meeting list reads: agree on the conflict resolution process and present the escalation procedure. B states exactly that. A is the strongest distractor because it simply swaps the two verbs, and the distinction matters: the team negotiates and agrees how it will handle conflict, whereas the escalation procedure follows from the project's **Governance Model** and is only presented. The **Project Handbook** and **Project Work Plan** are likewise presented rather than agreed at this meeting.
changes: new item

question: The Minutes of Meeting (MoM) of an Executing Kick-off Meeting summarise the issues raised, risks identified, decisions taken and changes proposed. According to the guide, what else must be done with those items?

options.A: They must be formally approved by the Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: They must each be added as a new task in the baselined Project Work Plan
options.C: They must be reported in the first Project Progress Report of the phase
options.D: They must also be entered in the relevant project logs, not only the MoM

explanation: The after-the-meeting step says the minutes should include a summary of issues raised, risks identified, decisions taken and changes proposed, and notes that these items should also be recorded in the relevant logs. That means the **Risk Log**, **Issue Log**, **Decision Log** and **Change Log**, so D is right. B is the tempting distractor: only significant issue-management or risk-response work is later reflected in the **Project Work Plan**, and the log entry comes first in every case.
changes: new item

question: A Business Manager (BM) offers to carry out some of the project's Quality Assurance activities. What does the PM² Guide say about this?

options.A: Quality Assurance may only be performed by the Project Quality Assurance (PQA) role
options.B: The Business Manager (BM) is one of the roles that may perform these activities
options.C: Quality Assurance may only be performed by the PM and external audit entities
options.D: The Business Manager (BM) may only perform quality control, never assurance

explanation: The **Quality Assurance** section says these activities can be performed by the **Project Manager (PM)**, the **Project Quality Assurance (PQA)** role, or other project roles such as the **Project Core Team (PCT)**, the **Business Manager (BM)** or the **Solution Provider (SP)**, and that external audits may also be defined. So the offer is entirely in line with the guide and B is correct. A is the strongest distractor: the **PQA** establishes the assurance standards and reviews outputs and deliverables, but it holds no monopoly on performing the work. All of these activities are documented in the **Quality Management Plan**.
changes: new item

question: Quality Assurance activities are documented in the Quality Management Plan. According to the Quality Assurance guidelines, which other artefact must these activities be part of?

options.A: The Project Work Plan
options.B: The Project Handbook
options.C: The Quality Review Report
options.D: The Outsourcing Plan

explanation: The guidelines are explicit: the **Quality Assurance** activities must be part of the **Project Work Plan**, so that they are scheduled and resourced like any other project work. That makes A correct.
